speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to refer the Insurance Bill which is now being considered by the Senate to the Supreme Court in order to obtain a decision as to its constitutionality? There was a rumour to that effect when a judgment was rendered by Mr. Justice Leith at Montreal a couple of months ago in the case of King vs. Witlis, Fabre & Company to the effect that that legislation was unconstitutional. It seems that it would be an advantage to find out the opinion of the highest court on that subject before we go more fully into the study of the proposed Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: $21,491,340 FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION RE COMPANIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the interesting question to which the hon. member has called your attention is but one phase of a larger question as to the powers respectively of the Dominion parliament and of' the local legislatures in regard to the incorporation of companies. That question was not long since raised for the decision of the Supreme Court, and the members of that court differed among themselves very decidedly in the opinions they expressed. The question being of such large practical importance, communication was had from the department of which I am in charge with the Attorneys General of the various provinces with a view to arriving, if possible, at some means by which these difficult and very weighty questions of the construction of the British North America Act may be definitely settled. That correspondence has resulted in a proposition from several of the provinces that a conference on the subject be had between representatives of the provinces and representatives of the Dominion government and such a conference is being arranged for. Communications are now being addressed to the various lieutenant governors of the different provinces proposing a meeting of representatives of the provinces and of the Dominion government to discuss the -whole subject, not the mere question of in-Mr. GRAHAM.
surance legislation but the larger one as to the right to incorporate companies in the provinces and in the Dominion respectively.

As the naval debate is to be resumed to-day I beg to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the following paragraph in the Toronto 'Globe' of February 4, referring to the Prime Minster's speech:
Its conclusion was marked by the inspiring spectacle of the whole House rising and singing the National Anthem.
The House knows that the inspiring spectacle referred to took place at the conclusion of the speech of my friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). I am not saying for one moment that this statement was sent out intentionally, but in view of the fact that it was given prominence not only in the recognized organization of the Liberal party but also in the Hamilton 'Times', the St. John 'Sun', the St. John 'Telegraph', the Halifax 'Chronicle', the Montreal 'Daily Herald', the Belleville 'Daily Ontario', the London 'Advertiser', the St. Thomas 'Journal' and the Winnipeg 'Free Press' and in view also of the fact that the Prime Minister was very severe last session on the immorality of false telegrams, I think I am voicing the sentiment of everybody on this side, and I am sure also of many on the other side, when I say we should be glad to have some little statement from the right hon. gentleman.

THE EDWARD MEDAL-HEROISM OF CONDUCTOR REYNOLDS.
speechtext: I desire to point out to the government that by warrant under the Royal Sign Manual of the 13th day of July, 1907, His Majesty created a new medal to be entitled the Edward medal to be awarded for heroic acts performed by miners, quarrymen and others who endanger their own lives in endeavouring to save the lives of others from perils in mines and quarries. And, by a further warrant, under His Majesty's Royal Sign Manual, on date of 1st of December, 1909, it is provided that this medal shall be awarded to those who, in the course of industrial employment, endanger their own lives in endeavouring to save the lives of others from perils incurred in connection with such industrial employment. I would ask the government whether this medal can be awarded to those who perform acts of heroism in saving the lives of others who are engandered in connection with the work of the railways of this country? The reason why I ask is that a very notable act of heroism has been performed by a conductor of the Canadian Pacific railway, Conductor Thomas Reynolds, who, at the risk of his own life and with unexampled courage, succeeded in saving the lives of nine others who had been imprisoned in the dining car which fell into the river and through the ice in the recent accident on the Sault line. If this medal could be awarded in connection with such acts of heroism, I earnestly hope that the government will bring Mr. Reynolds' signal heroism to the attention of the imperial authorities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE EDWARD MEDAL-HEROISM OF CONDUCTOR REYNOLDS.
speechtext: I am sure that hon. members will agree that, if any are entitled to medals for heroism, Conductor Reynolds stands at the head of their number. There is a society which generally looks after these things, and calls the attention of the government to acts of heroism. As soon as we have received such recommendation, we shall be glad to call the matter to the attention of the proper authorities.

House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the second reading of Bill (No. 95), respecting the Naval Service of Canada, the proposed amendment of Mr. Borden, and the amendment to the amednment of Mr. Monk thereto.

In rising to address the House on a subject of such vital importance to Canada, involving, as it does, not only our present status, but our future relation to the empire, I believe, upon the conclusion of this debate, we will have reached and passed an epoch marking mile-stone in the history, of the Dominion of Canada; and I believe that it is our bounden duty, our paramount duty, indeed, to consider not only whether the Bill before the House meets the requirement of the naval defence of Canada, but also whether it will tend to lead either to the consolidation or disintegration of the empire. A word or two first with reference to the question of militarism. I desire to place myself on record as not being in any manner a champion of the spirit of militarism. The question we are considering i3 simply a question of defence; it is not a question of aggression; it is not a question of doing anything towards the acquisition of territory; it is purely and simply a question of strengthening the central armament of the'empire, for the purpose of preserving peace as we have had it preserved during the last hundred years. And I make the statement that, the supremacy of the British navy, the unchallenged supremacy of that navy, has been the cause of our peace



for over a century. We know that peace has been the constant and devoted companion of Great Britain's supremacy on the sea of time for the greater part of a century; and we know that so soon as the supremacy of Britain upon the seas is menaced upon the international horizon appear war clouds and rumours of war. We know that because of the threatening of that supremacy through the naval progress of the greatest military power in Europe to-day, we have, for the first time, the threatened Armageddon. We have New Zealand making a magnificent offer of a Dreadnought ' ; we have Australia contributing to the empire a unit of the imperial navy. And it is because of these circumstances that we to-day are considering the question of naval defence. So, in speaking of this matter, in defending any form of naval defence, I am doing it because I believe that in strengthening, of the forces of the empire we are maintaining the peace not only of the colonies of Britain, but of the nations of the world. It has been the expressed policy of British statesmen, time and again, that the object of their navy is not for territorial aggression or anything of that kind, but simply for the preservation of peace. I would like to read to the House the words of the British Foreign Secretary, spoken last June before the imperial pres3 conference to show what the foreign policy of Great Britain is on this question. Sir Edward Grey said:
And I would say this: tile foreign policy of this country is to keep what we have got, to consolidate it, and develop it, to quarrel as little as possible with other people in doing so, and to uphold in the councils of the world in diplomacy those ideals in every part of the world by which we set so much store at home.
This is nothing more or less than the policy of, ' what we have we'll hold.' And I think we are quite justified in contributing in some measure to a policy of that kind.
The first question that occurs to one is what have we to hold? We have, I think I am safe in saying, an empire unrivalled in the history of the world. It is an empire of 400,000,000 souls, that is to say one-fifth the population of the globe; an empire that covers 12,000,000 square miles, or one-fifth the area of the globe. Of the entire population, 60,000,000 are Anglo-Saxon; 44,000,000 reside in the ' little isles in the foggy sea,' and 16,000,000 are scattered throughout the colonies of the empire. And, of the whole territory of 12,000,000 square miles, onlv 120,000 square miles are comprised within Great Britain itself. In that respect it is entirely different from all other empires of ancient or modern times. It is an empire of all climes, of all races, of all classes, of all creeds, of all longitudes, of all latitudes, of all sea3, and in that respect it is entirely different from any of the empires of ancient Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
or modern times. The Macedonian empire, the Assyrian empire, the Eoman empire, the Russian empire and all other gTeat empires were contiguous and continuous. Their geographical position was such that an army could be landed on one portion of the empire and could march to any other portion. How different it. is with the British empire to-day, which is divided by so many seas. But notwithstanding the fact that it is separated by these seas, there is no doubt that the various portions of the empire to-day are four or five times nearer to Great Britain than they were a hundred years ago, because time and distance have been almost annihilated by reason of present facilities of intercommunication in the shape of steamships, telegraphs, cables, wireless telegraphy, and probably in a short time, by reason of an aerial communication. For these reasons then we have the more cause for upholding that which is the all essential to the preservation of the empire, namely, naval supremacy upon the sea. Now, I make this formal statement that the existence of the British empire and of all her colonial dependencies depend upon the actual supremacy of the British navy upon the seas.
We ore apt to forget what it is costing Great Britain to maintain that supremacy, we forget it because we do not pay a single cent towards the maintenance of that supremacy, either on land or sea, although we obtain all the advantages, and all. the benefits and all the prestige and protection which we would obtain were we citizens of Great Britain herself. We are apt to forget, I say, what it is costing the mother country to-day in order to maintain that supremacy. Take the case of the British navy. What is Great Britain paying to-day for the maintenance of her navy? I think the annual naval estimate for 1910 is $75,000,000, that is $480,000 for every single day of the 365 days of the year. Now, I maintain that we, as a colony of Great Britain, are getting me advantage and protection of that expenditure of money just as fully and just as effectually as any citizen of Great Britain herself, and we are not contributing one cent thereto. In addition to that, she is maintaining a great standing army which is costing her $430,000 a day. It may be said, perhaps, that we do not get the same benefit from that army as do the citizens of Great Britain herself. But we must remember that it is the British navy that bears the British army upon its back; and if we were attacked in Canada by any great power, say that of the United States, for instance, we could depend upon the British navy to bear the British armies to our defence. So in that respect, without the supremacy of the British navy, the British army is of

no practical use to this country. With the supremacy of the British navy we receive the same benefit from her armv as any other portion of the empire or as Great Britain herself. Moreover, it is a matter of history that for the last 150 years, all the wars which Great Britain has fought have been fought across seas, and its troops have been borne across seas on the back of the navy, and all this money and treasure have been expended in fighting the battles
o.f distant portions of the empire.
We do not lack for illustrations of that. We have seen Great Britain send out into Persia an army for the purpose of relieving certain of her citizens who had been maltreated and imprisoned by the Persian emperer. When Canada herself was faced by the first rebellion in the Northwest, Great Britain sent out a body of troops wholly at her expense for the purpose of suppressing that rebellion. We know that when the rights and privileges of a certain number of citizens in South Africa were menaced, Great Britain did not hesitate at once to send out an army of 300,000 men from her shores; with the assistance and by means of British naval supremacy the navy was able to carry upon its back that army of 300,000 men, and to protect the ships and transports bearing provisions for them into South Africa. Of those troops,
18,000	never came back, and 65,000 or 70,000 bear to-day upon their persons the scars of that war; and not one cent was contributed before that time by South Africa tow'ards imperial defence. Now, Sir, we know that Great Britain would do exactly as she did in South Africa in case Canada were menaced in like manner; in other words, we would receive the benefit of the army and navy upon which she expends over $900,000 a day for the purpose of maintaining the integrity of the empire of which Canada forms a part.
Now let me illustrate that in another way. Supposing you went into the office of the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, and you wanted to know what that war in South Africa has cost. You look upon the credit side, and you see a precedent created that, no matter *where a British subject is found, once his rights have been invaded, Great Britain will at all costs fly to his rescue. On the debit side you will find 18,000 men -who have lost their lives, and you will find throughout Great Britain many a hearth and many a home that now

Asd the sound of the voice that is still.
You will find in addition to that, 65,000 or 70,000 men who went out to fight the battles of the empire, bearing upon their person the imperial phylacteries of devotion and loyalty to the motherland. You will find in addition that, in the office of the 102J
Chancellor of the Exchequer, on the debit side, a war costing $1,000,000,000, and you will find the Chancellor of the Exchequer raising at three per cent $30,000,000 every year for the purpose of paying the interest on that part of the national debt incurred by the South African war. Is that not a proof that we would derive the same_ benefit, and would derive the same material assistance, were national complications to arise between Canada and any foreign nation? We have that precedent of British assistance in South Africa, and we have the right to assume that she -would do the same thing for Canada.
Then, if we consider the matter from a totally selfish and material standpoint as it affects our own country, what do we find? We have here a coast lying on the Atlantic and on the Pacific oceans wholly unprotected. We have a number of thriving cities upon those two coast lines, wholly unprotected except by virtue of the supremacy of the British navy to-day. We enjoy the advantage, the prestige and the protection of all the diplomatic and consular service throughout the world, and it is unnecessary to say that such service is the greatest in the world. We know that Great Britain is paying to-day over $3,000,000 a year for her diplomatic and consular service alone, and we are getting the benefit of that as effectually as any other citizen of the British empire, while not contributing one cent towards it. Now, I make this broad statement, that Canada is rapidly growing, and as the increase in her commerce is going to be to a large extent an increase in her natural products, and as in that respect Canada will have a surplus of agricultural products, and as that surplus would go, not to the United States, but to countries beyond the seas which cannot now raise enough agricultural products for their own needs, it follows that as our trade increases, and as our export of agricultural products increases, the surplus for export must cross the seas, and in order to protect that vast commerce, we must have the supremacy of the British navy. The whole question resolves itself into this, that an invincible imperial navy is nothing more or less than an insurance policy insuring every portion of the empire against the contingency and horrors of war, and is a guarantee to each part of the empire of its peace, progress and prosperity.
Now let me say a word or two in reference to the speeches of the Right Hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon.. Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux). As to the character of the speeches, were I to look upon them from the standpoint of eloquence and rhetoric, I would say that they were par excellence. Both of these hon. gentlemen read quotations and extracts from the speeches of many eminent politicians, statesmen and

ecclesiastics. No douibt they did this for the purpose of suiting the political exigencies of these hon. gentlemen in various parts of the country. I do not know that it was necessary to go back and read these quotations from these gentlemen, many of whom had been dead for generations, some of whom have been dead for centuries, and I think it was rather a rude thing that they should go back and disturb Peter the Hermit from the peaceful hermitage where he has so long slumbered. What had all this to do with the question at issue? The question at issue is whether Canada, by reason of its position in the empire to-day, or by reason of the impending difficulties and necessities which beset the empire, _ is going to make a contribution to imperial defence, and, if so, what is to be the manner of making that contribution? Upon that aspect of the case I say that the precedents which the First Minister and the Postmaster General have quoted are wholly irrelevant to the matter at issue, because the matter at issue is simply the question of a voluntary gift by this government to the mother country for the purpose of assisting her in the difficulties which have beset her, and there is no constitutional authority which has anything to do with the question of whether we choose to make a gift to the mother country for the purpose of strengthening our national defence. I see upon the OTder paper a resolution authorizing the government to make a grant of $50,000 to the city of Paris for the purpose of aiding those who have suffered by reason of the recent flood which has taken place in that city. With that I am quite in accord, but why would it be necessary for any one to get up and cite constitutional authorities as to whether we should or should not grant to the city of Paris something to relieve the present situation? Yet, such an argument would be on all fours with the argument put up by these hon. gentlemen in regard to the navy.
But, I would not have found so much fault with the speeches of these hon. gentlemen, and especially with the speech of the right hon. the First Minister, if the right hon. gentleman had confined himself to what was the policy of his own party, though, no doubt, there was great reason to find fault with that. What did the First Minister say? He said:
This policy is in the best traditions of the Liberal party. This policy is the latest link in the long chain of events which followed from the principles laid down by the reformers of the old times, Baldwin and Lafontaine, which, step by step, stage by stage, have brought Canada to the position it now occupies, that is to say, the rank, dignity and status of a nation within the British empire.
He was not satisfied with that, but further he went on to say:

I am bound to say at the same time that it has been censured and criticised-severely censured and severely criticised-by those who within the party boast of their imperialism, who carry abroad upon their foreheads the imperial phylacteries, who boldly walk into the temple and there loudly thank the lord that they are not like other British subjects, that they give tithes of everything they possess, and that in them alone is to be found the true incense of loyalty.
The right hon. gentleman has been leading the Liberal party for about twenty years, and had the policy which he has advocated been canned into effect it would have led us, according to the right hon. gentleman, to the position we occupy to-day as the first colony in the British empire, the brightest jewel in the British Crown! Well, I think that the right hon. gentleman, having made this statement, it is only fair and just to this side of the House that I should see whether the policies which he heretofore advocated would have led us to'the position we occupy to-day. I do not need to go back a century, I do not need to go back more than twenty years, it is within the memory of the youngest member of this House, to compare the policies which the right hon. gentleman has enunciated within the last twenty years with the position we occupy to-day. Less than twenty years ago the right hon. gentleman advocated several distinct anti-British trade policies. The right hon. gentleman first advocated continental freedom of trade, then unrestricted reciprocity, and then commercial union. We all remember that upon the platforms of this country the right hon. gentleman said time and again: Place, me in power and I will give -you continental free trade, unrestricted reciprocity, or commercial union. We know that if the country had taken him at his word and placed him in power we would have had either commercial union or unrestricted reciprocity. It goes without saying that had the right hon. gentleman thrown down the customs barriers which then existed and which exist now between this country and the great nation to the south of us, the first step would have been commercial union, and the next step would have been political union. During all that time, while these anti-British policies were being advocated by the right hon. gentleman and his followers, the Conservative party, led by that grand, old, patriotic, loyal chieftain, Sir John A. Macdonald, said: We will have none of it. Sir John Macdonald consistently and persistently argued and preached the gospel that the destiny of this country was inseparably bound up with that of the motherland. It was upon that policy, upon that issue that he uttered those famous words: A British subject I was born, a British subject I will die. Imbued with these. anti-British policies the right hon. the leader of the government passed over to the

most literary city upon the other side of the line, to the city of Boston, and he gave utterance to his opinion eighteen or twenty years ago. What was his opinion there? Were his opinions there such as, had they been carried out, would have led us to the position we occupy to-day as the brightest jewel in the British Crown, or were they such as, had they been carried out, would have made us an independent nation? I will quote what the right hon. gentleman said:
The conduct of England and Canada during the civil war of 1861-66 was a disgrace to the civilization of England and Canada. [DOT] t - It is a great, a fatal mistake to make allegiance, British allegiance, the basis of trade. . . The present position of Canada cannot last, even at this day England and Canada have interests totally apart, and that the time will come when in the very nature of things separation must take place. I am a subject oi the British Crown, but whenever I have to choose between the interests of England and of Canada, it is manifest to me that the interests of my country are identical with the interests of the United States of America.
Then, Sir, being subsequently tiwitted with these assertions by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) on the floor of this House, being asked if he still maintained these views, because there are occasions sometimes when a man will say in the heat of the moment and before a public audience perhaps what he does not really mean; but, when these statements were cast up to the right hon. gentleman on the floor of this House did he repudiate them? I say: No, and we will see what he said on the floor of this House. He said:
He (Mr. Foster) speaks as if Canada were to remain for ever a colony. Light as our dependence may be on the mother country, that dependence is not to remain for ever. If we were to admit that, if we were to say that we were always to remain in a dependent condition we would be the scorn of the world and it would be scorn well deserved. . . It is the destiny of the colonies to become nations as it is the destinty of a child to become a man, and while no doubt the idea of separation from the motherland *causes a pang in the heart no doubt of every one, yet there is not a child who leaves his father's house who does not do so without a pang if his heart is in the proper place. .	. I have
again and again repeated that the goal of my aspiration is the independence of Canada, to see Canada an independent nation in course of time. If we were true to our record we will again exhibit to the world, the unique, the unprecedented example of a nation achieving its own independence by slow degrees and as naturally as the severing of the ripe fruit from the parent tree. . . The Minister of Finance reproached me a moment ago, that I had stated at Boston that the Canadian people had commercial interests different from the British people. Sir, I said so in Boston and I say so now on the floor of this House.
That was. the policy advocated by the
right hon. gentleman away back in these days. Let us follow him down to the present day. The next instance that arose to elicit an expression of the right hon. gentleman's imperialism was the South African war. Remember, he has just a few days ago said on the floor pf the House:	'I do not pretend
to say that I am an imperialist,' and that is the frankest admission we have had from him so far. Now, when the trouble broke out in South Africa, when little New Zealand was the first to make her offer to send troops to assist the motherland, when Australia and all the other colonies followed suit, men were wondering what was the matter with Canada and the answer from the right hon. gentleman was:	'I do not
think I can send troops to South Africa, I do not think I have the power.' But, the . newspapers of this country reflected public opinion, and to them great credit is due, and I particularly mention the Montreal ' Star,' because the Montreal ' Star ' sent telegraphic despatchees to the mayors of every city and town in the Dominion with the purpose of ascertaining the true sentiment of the Dominion, and. the practically Unanimous answer was:	By all means
send troops to South Africa and assist the mother country for there may come a day when we ourselves will need just such assistance. From the confines of the two oceans there started a great wave of patriotic loyal sentiment gathering force as it went along, until finally it thundered against the doors of this parliament, and then and then only the right hon. gentleman awoke from his imperial slumber to find that he could do what he before said it was impossible to do under the constitution, namely send a contingent to South Africa. He realized then that the question was of such magnitude that if there was not a precedent, Canada was bound to create a precedent, and I say Sir, at the present time if there is no precedent for what the Conservative party propose should be done, we are bound to create a precedent. So that whatever credit or prestige and advantage which Canada obtained from her participation in the South African war is not due to the right hon. gentleman himself, but to the patriotism, loyalty and. devotion of the Canadian people, and to that irresistible wave of loyal sentiment which passed over this country and which forced the right hon. gentleman against his own convictions to send Canadian troops to South Africa. We now pass to the imperial conference of 1907. Up to that time the right hon. gentleman was free to act as he chose; if he were an imperialist and desired to do something which would show his practical interest in the motherland and his desire to contribute towards the deI fence of the empire he could have moved

in that direction at this conference. But, not only did he not move, but he took a step which clearly expresses the sentiment which he himself has stated a few days ago in this House, namely:	'I do
not prtetend to be ;an imperialist.' What occurred at that conference? Dr. Smart introduced a resolution. If that resolution had said that the overseas Dominions must contribute in a certain manner; if the resolution had said: You must give so much money, or you must build a local fleet, or you must give two ' Dreadnoughts ' to the British navy, there might be some excuse for the right hon. gentleman not agreeing with the resolution. But, the resolution was so fair and so reasonable that I shall read it:
_ That this conference, recognizing the vast importance of the services rendered by the navy to the defence of the empire and the protection of its trade, and the paramount importance of continuing to mainain the navy in the highest possible state of efficiency, considers it to be the duty of the dominions beyond the seas to make such contributions towards the upkeep of the navy as may be determined by their local legislatures-the contributions to take the form of a grant of money, the establishment of local naval defence, or such other services, in such manner as may be decided upon after consultation with the admiralty and as would best accord with varying circumstances.
That is the resolution and it says in effect, that it is the duty of the different portions of the empire to do what they may deem the best in the way of a contribution towards assisting the motherland in the imperial defence, and yet the right hon. gentleman dissented and said he would have nothing to do with it. It is in line with the sentiment he expressed in the House the other day when he said:	I am
not an imperialist. Well, matters remained in that position until something occurred and when that something occurred did the right hon. gentleman act on his own volition? No. The hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) put upon the order paper a resolution, which said in effect: it is time we should do something towards assisting the motherland in relieving her of the burden of defence. It was a move from this side of the House, and following it came the emergency and the pressure of public opinion again. The newspapers, reflecting public opinion, showed that Canadians believed that Canada must do something to assist the motherland in the crisis, and under pressure the right hon. gentleman consented to the adoption of a resolution having for its object the giving of a contribution to the motherland for the purpose of assisting in the defence of the empire. That resolution was passed in March, 1909, and the right hon. gentleman sent over delegates to the conference Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
in the old country and they' brought back the proposition which we have before the House. When he submitted that proposition to the parliament in the first place he said: This navy shall not go to the assistance of Great Britain until the parliament of Canada is called. Again public opinion as expressed in the press demonstrated that the people of Canada would not stand for that, and when the right hon. gentleman came before us next time his declaration was: This navy may go to war and parliament need not be called but it shall not go to war until this government says it shall, and if it does go to war then parliament shall be called. To that extent he receded from his former position, but he gave way mightly little, because it simply means that if the right hon. gentleman sits still, as he did in the South African war, if he does nothing, as he said he would have done in the case of the Crimean war, then nothing is done and parliament is not called and Canada does not .go to the assistance of the empire. I would like to put this proposition to the right hon. gentleman: Suppose Great Britain took the same stand he has taken; suppose Great Britain said to us exactly as he has said to Great Britain I do not'pretend to be an imperialist!, the inevitable conclusion is that if Canada should get into difficulties we would not or could not expect to receive one particle of assistance from the motherland. Now, what is the position of Australia? The other day when our honored leader was making some remarks, on the position Australia had taken with reference to her naval unit, the Minister of Militia rose in his seat and said, that from the report contained in the imperial conference it appeared that the Australian parliament had to consent to its fleet going to war before it could go to war. Am I right in that? At any rate while I do not pretend to be as familiar with this question as the hon. Minister of Militia is, I take it that the passage to which the Minister of Militia refers is that contained at page 57 of the imperial conference report:
In peace time and while on the Australian station this fleet unit would be under the exclusive control of the Commonwealth government as regards their movements and general administration, but officers and men should be governed bv regulations similar to the King's regulations, and be under naval discipline, and when with vessels of the Royal navy, the senior officer should take command of the whole. Further, when placed by the Commonwealth government at the disposal of the admiralty in war time, the vessels should be under the control of the naval commander-vn-chief.
Now, because this memorandum says that the Australian fleet unit may in war time be placed by the Australian Commonwealth at the disposal of the admiralty,

the hon. Minister of Militia -says that the parliament of the Commonwealth must first consent to its being placed on actual war service, if I may so put it. What I say is that that meanis when so placed in the manner mentioned in paragraph 8 of the memorandum submitted by Australia to the conference, which paragraph is to be found at .page 5, and reads thus:
8. In time of war or emergency or upon a declaration by the senior naval officer representing British government, that a condition of emergency exists, all the vessels of the naval force of the Commonwealth shall be placed by the Commonwealth government under the orders of Lords ComAissioners of the admiralty. Tne method by which the vessels shall come under the orders of the senior naval officer would be by furnishing each commander of an Australian vessel with sealed orders and instructions (to) the effect that upon the declaration to him by the senior naval officer representing British government that a state of war or emergency exists, such sealed orders shall thereupon be opened, and, in pursuance of their provisions, he shall thereupon immediately place himself under the orders of the senior naval officer representing the British government.
Now, to prove that that is correct, I read the next paragraph, which states the only exception made to that provision:
It is, however, to be understood that if the services of any of the coast defence vessels be desired in seas remote from Australia, the approval of the Commonwealth government shall first be obtained to their removal.
In other words, the approval of the Commonwealth government is not to be first obtained for the service of any vessels except coast defence vessels. An armoured cruiser is not a coast defence vessel, it is intended to go on the high seas and make an aggressive movement. Therefore, the hon. gentleman is not right in his contention that the -assent of the_ Commonwealth government is to be obtained^ before the Australian unit can be used in the defence of the empire, because the memorandum which was placed before the conference by Australia says that in case of war it shall be immediately placed under the command of the senior officer of the admiralty.
I sometimes wonder whether hon. gentlemen on the other -side of the House really understand the meaning of this Bill. As I understand, the right hon. leader the government's position is that this is purely a voluntary gift on the part of this country, and that we may accompany it with any conditions we choose. The right hon. gentleman says, I will not now agree to trust to Great Britain for one hour as to whether or not we shall assist her in case of war; I reserve to myself the absolute right and privilege of saying, after the war has commenced, whether it is such a war as I can countenance, and whether, in view_ of the circumstances, I can come to the assistance of the mother country. I say that that position taken by the right hon. gentleman is a less loyal and less patriotic position, and displays less trust and confidence in the motherland, than the position of an ordinary independent ally, who says:	In
case of war I will trust you and come to your assistance. Here is the position of Japan in the treaty made^ with Great Britain five years ago and which is in force to-day:
The governments of Great Britain and Japan, being desirous of replacing the agree-meut concluded between them on the 30tli of January, 1902, bv fresh stipulations, have agreed upon the following articles, which have for their object-
If by reason of unprovoked attack or aggressive action, wherever arising, on the part of any other power or powers, either contracting party should be involved in war in defence of its territorial rights or special interests mentioned in the preamble of this agreement, the other contracting party wTill at once come to the assistance of its ally, and will conduct the war in common, and make peace in mutual agreement with it. .
Here is Japan, on the 12th of August, 1905, going to Great Britain and saying: I have enough trust and confidence in you now, that for the period of ten years I am going to bind myself, if you become involved in war at any time during that period, to come to your assistance. In that respect I say the proposition of the Prime Minister is less loyal and less patriotic than the position of Japan in that treaty. The right hon. gentleman charges us with bearing imperial phylacteries on our hrows^ and walking boldly into the temple and there proclaiming that we are not as other British subjects are. I can only say that we are willing to go into the temple and proclaim that we are not as other British subjects are if that is the kind of imperialism with which right hon. gentleman is imbued.
Now, let us come to the question of emergency; and I want to point out that in the Bill before the House, and in the speech he made on that Bill, the right hon. the Prime Minister has entirely overlooked the circumstances which have brought that Bill to this House. That Bill would not have been before this House to-day, I venture to say, unless a condition of emergency had existed in Europe; and yet the right hon. gentleman, in bringing the Bill into the House, totally disregards the very reason for that Bill, by failing to make any provision whatever for the emergency which has caused it. He admits himself that it will be five years-I venture to say that it will be- ten years before a single ship of the Canadian navy will be completed, equipped, manned and ready to do her part in active service. According to the best experts in Europe the crisis is going to come within the next ten years, and we are making no provision to meet

it, although it is the very reason for this Bill being before this House. By an emergency I do not mean a present actual, crisis. I mean a condition of things which, if allowed to proceed in the manner determined upon, will eventually and inevitably lead to the destruction of that which is allessential, both to ourselves and to the British empire, the supremacy of the British navy at sea. If we find a condition of things existing to-day which, if allowed to continue, will bring us to that culmination, I call that an emergency, and it is upon that I propose to make my argument now. Let me point first of ail to this fact, that ten years ago the German nation decided that they should have a very power-M navy. A Bill was brought into the Eeichstag appropriating $l,uu0,000,000 for the purpose of starting their naval programme. Since that time they have not only kept up that programme, but have accelerated it by increasing the appropriation by $500,000,000, part of it in 1906 and part in 1908. Since that time there has arisen in the Eeichstag what is known as the 'Expansionist party,' who are in favour of increasing German armaments. We know they are increasing German armaments. We know that the German nation is to-day increasing in population at the rate of about 900,000 every year. I do not mean to say that the German people are not right in taking the stand they do. If by their sacrifice, their perseverance and their energy they are able to place the German fleet on a par with the British fleet, they have a perfect right to do so, and looking at the matter from their standpoint, it is a credit to them that they do so. At the same time the same reasoning applies to us, and if we are weak enough to allow them to do that we have nobody to thank but ourselves.
Now take the German construction; compare the German construction to-day with the German construction ten years ago, and what do we find? We find that- the German construction to-day is $36,000,000 more than it was ten years ago. The British con struction to-day is only ten millions more than it was ten years ago. The total annual naval expenditure of Germany has increased in the last five years by $47,000,000. The total annual naval expenditure of Great Britain has increased only _ $10,000,000. Then we have this very significant fact that by reason of the advent of the Dreadnought type of armoured cruiser, all types prior to that have been practically relegated to the scrap heap. We have the authority of the Et. Hon. Eeginald McKenna, First Lord of the Admiralty, for that statement. He said in the imperial House of Commons:
There will come a day when, by an almost automatic process, all ships of an earlier type Mr. MIDDLEBEO.
than the Dreadnought will be relegated to the scrap heap. The maintenance of our superiority then will depend upon our superiority in Dreadnoughts alone. The German power of constructing this particular type of vessel is at this time almost if not fully equal to our own, owing to their rapid development within the past eighteen months.
If that is the case, it means that the greater part of the German navy will be' essentially more powerful than the British navy, because the greater part of the German navy not being as old as the British navy will be constructed of the modern type. _
I wish to refer to a speech made by the right hon. the Prime Minister in Toronto not long ago, I think on the 6th of January 1910. He said:
However, in the province of Ontario another position is taken-I will not say by the whole of the Conservative party-that we should make at once a contribution to the British navy, that we should contribute at once, one to three Dreadnoughts, that we should contribute at once thirty million dollars. The cause, they say, for this urgency is that danger is imminent for Britain. Danger? Where is it coming from? They tell us from Germany Let us look at this. We know that the displacement of the British navy is nearly two million tons, and that of the German navy is_ six hundred thousand tons. In 1912 the British navy will have a displacement oi more than two million tons, and the German navy one of about a million tons. So that the disparity is too great to say that danger is imminent.
The right hon. gentleman brushes aside the question of emergency with the statement that because in 1912 the German navy will have a tonnage of only 1,000,000 tons, whereas the British navy will have a tonnage of 2,000,000 tons, therefore, the question of emergency cannot arise. I would point out to the right hon. gentleman that according to his own statement there will be a difference of 400,000 tons between the German navy now, and the German navy in 1912. That means that in the space of two years Germany will have added to her navy
400,000	tons. Divide that into Dreadnoughts, that is by 20,000 tons, and it means 20 Dreadnoughts. Now, supposing I cut off 25 per cent of that and make it 15, it will mean that Germany will have 15 Dreadnoughts built in the next two years. Then I take the statements of the Et. Hon. Mr. McKenna, First Lord of the Admiralty, and the Et. Hon. Sir Edward Grey, who say that if you build 15 Dreadnoughts you must relegate to the scrap heap all of the preDreadnought type, and so the 400,000 tons which the Germans will add to their navy in the next few years will be worth four or five times the same tonnage of the old obsolete British warship. It is not tonnage that counts, it is the class of vessel, the range of guns, the protection of the cruiser,

and last but not least, the efficiency of officers and men. We have abundant illustrations of that. It was not because the Russian fleet in the Japanese sea was so inferior in tonnage, it was not inferior, but it was that the Japanese fleet was modern, up to date and equipped with modern guns. That battle as we know lasted only forty minutes. It was not that the tonnage _ of Spain was so inferior, it was the superior guns and arms and the efficiency of the officers and men of iflie United States navy that sent the Spanish fleet to the bottom of the sea in a few minutes. So it is no argument to say that because the tonnage of the British fleet is greater than the tonnage of the German fleet there is no danger of war. The tonnage of the German fleet may be only half that of the British fleet, and still it may be a more eective fighting force than the whole British fleet.
Let us see what authority there is for the statement that there is an emergency. I do not think it is fair to the people of Canada for the Prime Minister and the Postmaster General to brush aside in a light manner, and with the levity displayed by them on this occasion, the question of emergency. Let us see what the greatest authorities in England themselves think of the emergency, let us take the opinion of men who know what they are talking about and who have given this matter serious consideration. You have heard our leader, in his speech on the second reading, state that Mr. McKenna had said in the House of Commons that all vessels prior to _ the Dreadnought type would be obsolete in a very short space of time and would have to be relegated to the scrap heap, and that Germany's power of construction is almost equal to our own. You have heard it stated that when the German programme is carried out she will have 33 Dreadnoughts, the most powerful fleet in the world, and as to the necessity of the entire rebuilding of preDreadnought fleets. You have heard the Liberal Prime Minister (Mr. Asquith) admit that by 1912 Germany would have at least 13 Dreadnoughts ready for service^ I propose now to give you some information given prior to the British elections. I do not propose to read, as the Postmaster General did, any utterance of the statesmen of Great Britain during the elections. Three months after the British House of Commons closed, at the Imperial Press Conference in June last, Lord Rosebery said: '
Now gentlemen, you will forgive me if I come next and at once to wliat is by far the most vital topic that you will have to discuss at this conference, or which concerns our empire as a whole-I means that of imperial defence. (Cheers.) I do not know that in some ways I have ever seen a condition of things in Europe so remarkable, so peaceful, and in some respects so ominous, as the condition which exists at this moment. There is a hush in Europe, a hush in which one might almost hear a leaf fall to the ground. There is an absolute absence of any questions which ordinarily lead to war. One of the great empires which is sometimes supposed to menace peace is entirely engrossed with its domestic affairs. Another great eastern empire which has furnished a perpetual problem for European statesmen has taken a new lease of life and youth in searching for liberty and constitutional reform. All, then, forbodes peace, and yet, at the same time, combined with this total absence of all question of friction, there never was, in the history of the world, so threatening and overpowering a preparation for war. That is the sign which I regard as most ominous. For forty years it has been a platitude to say that all Europe is an armed camp, and for forty years it has been true that all the nations have been facing each other armed to the teeth, and that has been, in some respects, a guarantee of peace. And now what do we see? And now, without any tangible reason, we see the nations preparing new armaments. They cannot, indeed, arm any more men upon land, so they have to seek new armaments upon the sea, piling up this enormous preparation, as if for some approaching Armageddon. And yet this is in the time of the profoundest peace. We live in the midst of what I think was called by Petrarch a ' latens helium '-a silent warfare, in which not a drop of blood is shed in anger, but in which the very last drop is extracted from the body by the lancets of the European statesmen. I admit there are features of this general preparation for war which must cause special anxiety to the friends of Great Britain and of the British empire.
When 1 see one country alone asking for Zt>
millions of extra taxation for warlike preparations ; when I see the unprecedented sacrifices which are asked from us on the same grounds, I do begin to feel uneasy as to the outcome of it all, and to wonder where it will stop. .	.	. Gentlemen, we can and we
will build ' Dreadnoughts ' or whatever the newest type of ship may be as long as we have a shilling to spend on them or a man to put into them. All that we can and will do, but I am not sure that even that will be enough, and I think it may be your duty to take back to your young dominions across the seas this message and this impression: that some personal dutv and responsibility for national defence rests on every man and citizen of the empire. Yes, gentlemen, take that message back with you. Tell your peoples - if they can believe it - the deplorable wav in which Europe is relapsing into militarism and the pressure that is put upon this little England, to defend itself, its liberties-and yours! But take this message also back with you-that the old country is right at heart; that there is no failing or weakness in her; and that she rejoices in renewing her youth in her giant dominions beyond the seas. For her own salvation, she must look to herself, and chat failing her she must look to you.
I cannot add anything to that. But I will quote now the opinion of Sir Edward Grey, who, as you know, is foreign secre-

tary. He spoke at this same conference. This was after the British parliament rose last March, and I may say that all these speeches were revised by the speakers themselves, except that of Bight Hon. Arthur J. Balfour, as stated in the preface of this Imperial Press Conference report itself, so that these are matured and clear expressed opinions of these eminent gentlemen :
Take the question of expenditure upon armaments. The other day, when we expressed our views of how serious the expenditure on armaments was becoming, there came at once, and in a way which admitted of no mistake, a response from other parts of the empire which made us feel that the empire beat with one heart. I would refer for a moment-merely to emphasize it-to the serious way in which Lord Bosebery spoke the other evening on this subject. I endorse every word he said. We are in comparatively calm weather, not in stormy weather, in foreign politics at the present moment, but the excessive expenditure on armaments makes the weather sultry. And the seriousness of that expenditure cannot be over-rated; but you should know to-day how conscious we are at home that we have far too much at stake to allow our naval expenditure to fall behind, however great the burden, and you from beyond the seas have made it clear to us 'how great the resources of the empire are. In upholding the empire surely we are going more and more towards the ideal to which Mr. Kirwan referred in his speech yesterday -of a union of allies-of self-governing dominions.
Then, Bight Hon. Beginald McKenna, First Ix>rd of the Admiralty, speaking at the same conference, said:
We look to the future and we see growing difficulties surrounding our empire. We foresee possibilities in which we should he called upon to unite our whole strength in a common defence.
Bight Hon. Alfred Lyttleton, who was colonial secretary in the previous government, said:
Well, my belief is, the actual position, the actual situation * of affairs at this moment is different from that which it has been since the battle of Trafalgar. We are in the presence for the first time of powers equal to ourselves in wealth, equal to ourselves in mechanical skill and efficiency, equal to ourselves in national self-consciousness and aspiration, unhappily superior to ourselves in population. As these things stand, unless fortune takes some unusual turn, I believe that Lord Rosebery spoke the absolute truth, and I was delighted to hear Sir Edward Grey on this occasion endorse what he said-that this country may always be relied upon to spend her last shilling if it is necessary for her own defence and for the defence of the empire, hut that a time might come when it would he necessary for her own safety and for their own safety that the dominions over seas should assist her in a tremendous struggle.
I firmly believe myself that the ultimate destiny and fate of this empire will depend-

must depend-upon the achievement of a really closer and more consolidated unity and a more perfect organization of defence.
Now, I will take the speech of the Bight Hon. Mr. Balfour, which appears at page 170 of the report of this Press Conference:
The fate of Australia, the fate of New Zealand, of Canada, South Africa, India, that is not going to he decided in the Pacific; it is not going to he decided in the Indian ocean; it is going to be decided here-and everybody who attempts to read the signs of the times will, I think, agree with the weighty words which fell from Lord Rosebery less than a week ago, and from Sir Edward Grey yesterday, and will recognize that no man can now speak on this subject of imperial defence without some note of anxiety in his voice. Not panic! There is no question, gentlemen, of panic, but we all have to look around us at the gathering forces, the arrangement of possible foes, the strategic import of possible combinations-we have got to look at them, not with a frightened but with a careful eye and, so looking at them, everybody, I think, will be impelled to recognize that the language of the foreign secretary-unusual, let me say, in the months of foreign secretaries-does not go beyond the necessities of the situation.
Now, take the great military authority, Lord Roberts, who is reported at page 179 of the report of this conference as saying:
Recent events, however, prove conclusively that a new era has commenced, and that our whole empire may again have to fight for its own, as the people of these islands have many times had to do in the past. The question is : Are we prepared to do this? Fleets and effective armies cannot be improvised to meet the rapid movements of modern times. Nothing but forethought and preparation, extending over years, can give us a naval or military strength which may be relied on in any great emergency, and which is in itself the greatest guarantee of that peace which we desire and need more than any other nation. I think I know what your main difficulty will be. It is not easy to convince the mass of the people in this country of the existence of real danger. It may be even less easy to convince the populace of colonies that have enjoyed for a century protection, which has given them security from attack, that real dangers threaten them also. . . The growth of the colonies in wealth makes them more and more objects of envy to nations which do not possess such valuable areas of the world. So, if we are to be secure, we must stand side by side in common effort and common sacrifice.
I will give only one more authority. I quote from the speech of Admiral Beres-ford, delivered in July last:
The first grave warnings that came before the public came from the lips of the Prime Minister and the Foreign Secretary, and those of the foreign secretary were even more serious than the Prime Minister. These warnings were often repeated by those respected and esteemed statesmen, Mr. Balfour and Sir Edward Grey. Sir Edward Grey considered the situation so grave and serious that

we must rebuild the whole fleet. In those words 1 agree, and I will endeavour to prove the Foreign Secretary was right.
And, after all this, we have the word of the right hon. Reginald McKenna, the Foreign Secretary Sir Ed. Grey and the Premier Mr. Asquith spoken in the House of Commons itself. After all these opinions, we come back again to the First Lord of the Admiralty speaking on July 26, 1909 in the House of Commons:
After very anxious careful examination of the conditions of shipbuilding in foreign countries, the government have come to the conclusion that it is desirable to take all necessary steps to ensure that the second four ships referred to in the programme shall be completed by March, 1912.
Now, I do not ask you to accept my word, but I say that we are bound to take the opinion of these gentlemen who know what they are talking about in preference to the opinion of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) and the right hon. leader of this House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). We find the Postmaster General stating this in his speech the other evening:
But we all know that this German scare exists only in the imagination of party politicians. It was started by the party press of Great Britain, controlled by Lord Northeliffe, and was written up during the elections by the well-known Socialist, Mr. Blatchford, in the pay of a certain party in Great Britain.
Well, does the Postmaster General honestly think that Sir Edward Grey, Lord Roseberry, Right Hon. Mr. Balfour, Prime Minister Asquith, Right Hon. Mr. McKenna, the first Lord of the Admiralty, Lord Roberts, probably the greatest military authority in the world, and Lord Charles Beresford, the greatest naval authority in Great Britain-does the Postmaster General really say now, after hearing the words of these gentlemen, that this scare was started for party purposes? But, in order to justify himself the Postmaster General goes on to say that the result of the British elections has answered the war scare.
By what manner of mathematical computation does the Postmaster General conclude that the British elections have answered the war scare, that the British elections do not show a popular belief in the existence of an emergency to-day? Take it any way the hon. gentleman chooses and he cannot show that. According to the press reports that have come back to this country, within the last few days his contention is not correct. Now, what do we find? The latest cable reports disclose that, excluding only those Irish constituencies in which a Nationalist was running against a Nationalist, or a Nationalist against a Unionist, the result of the polling in Great Britain shows that the Socialists, the Liberals and
the Labourites and Nationalists together obtained 2,847,893 votes, and the Unionists 3,080,072. So the whole electorate of Great Britain voted by a majority of 235,000 that there is something wrong with the administration of the admiralty of Great Britain. They have said bv a majority of 230,000 that there is an emergency. But I will take as further proof the candidature of Lord.*Char-les Beresford himself, and every body knows that he was and is a very vigorous exponent of the defects in the government s navy policy. It- was in consequence of his advocacy that the British government accelerated its naval programme. Lord Charles Beresford condemned the government for the inaction they had taken, as I have before pointed out and further, he said: We should spend $275,000,000 to $300,000,000 to increase the navy, and he went to the country upon that platform, and what was the result? He went to the constituency of Portsmouth where he and his running mate advocated the policy I have outlined, and what was the result? Not only in Portsmouth, but in the surrounding British cities on the coast opposite the continent of Europe the electors spoke. In Portsmouth they converted a government majority of 4,796 into an opposition majority of 7,575. The Postmaster General must not forget that the issue which Lord Charles Beresford presented to his constituents was the naval question almost exclusively, and upon that issue the people said by a turn over of 12,000 votes, we agree with him. In the two Davenport seats there was a reversal of 3,722 votes. In the three Bristol seats a former Liberal majority of 10,440 wa3 changed to a minority of 3,338. In West Bristol the Unionist majority of 365 was increased to 1,278. In Plymouth a Liberal majority of 2,857 was pulled down to 311. The government's majority in Southampton was curtailed, while the Unionist vote in Dover was increased. So wherever the test was applied upon the naval question, and the necessity of maintaining naval supremacy, the British electorate said in an unmistakable manner: We believe there is a crisis, and we believe the navy of Great Britain ought to be strengthened.
Now, what is the best means of strengthening the navy of Great Britain? I think I have proved that there is an emergency, I think I have shown a condition of things which, if not remedied, will culminate in the overthrow of British supremacy at sea. That being the case, what is the best means of meeting that emergency? Let me quote what Mr. Balfour says upon that question. On page 167 of the proceedings of the imperial press conference, 1909, Mr. Balfour expressed himself in this manner:
I think it is desirable and necessary that each of the self-governing constituents of the empire should consider whether it ought not, whether it must not, provide both land and sea forces to prevent raids, to prevent insult?

to their ports, and to see that they do not fall an easy prey to the first comer. But after all, gentlemen, local defence, though it be necessary, is really subordinate to imperial defence, and it is subordinate from the point of view of the localities themselves, not merely from the point of view of the empire as a whole. The individual constituents of the empire never can be safe, never can be powerful enough, never can be strong, whatever their local defence be, if that defence is only local. On the other hand, a serious menace to their independence is, I believe, quite impossible as long as the imperial system of defence is adequate, as long as we retain, as 1 hope we shall ever retain, that maritime predominance which is the very condition of our being.
Again at page 169:
The fate of the empire is not going to depend on that. The fate of the empire is going to depend upon the fleet power that we can bring against other fleet power, and that gives, if I may say so, to this country and to this quarter of the world, a strategic importance which otherwise it might not possess. We must-we inhabitants of these islands- we must for many years to come bear the main burden of imperial defence, because we are the largest population at present, and at present the wealthiest portion of the empire. We shall bear that burden cheerfully. But in addition to that reason for our special and peculiar position in the system of imperial defence, there is another depending on purely strategical and geographical considerations. If I am right-and I think all will agree I am right-that the fate of the empire depends on fleet superiority, that superiority must be shown in home waters. The German ocean, the channel, the neighbourhood of these islands, possibly the Mediterranean-those are the places at which, if there is to be an Armageddon, the Armageddon will take place, and it is folly for us to attempt, to dare, to dissipate these fleet constituents, so that when the time of crisis arises we shall not be able to have that concentration upon which our whole imperial destinies, and the destinies of each separate portion of the empire, really and substantially depend.
Now let us see what Mr. McKenna the First Lord of the British Admiralty, says upon this question of concentration. He says:
Tou will have your own views as to the proper development of defensive forces in your dominions. It is only by your working out your problems for yourselves that you can ever gain the experience which we have had to gain, and lessons that were told you from the experience of others would never come home to you with the same force as lessons that can be learned for yourselves, even though you have learned them through your own mistakes. We will assist in every way in our power, and whatever be the method by which we are asked to assist. And we are sure that in the long run out of this process of self-development every dominion will come ultimately to the same conclusion, that the naval problem of defence is one and the same the whole world over, and that the maintenance of supremacy in all seas alike.

Now let us see what Sir Edward Grey, Britain's Foreign Secretary, says:
The navy is the common security of the whole empire. If it ever fails to be that it will be of no use for us to discuss any other subjects, and the maintenance of the navy in that position, therefore, must be the first care, not only of us at home, but of the selfgoverning dominions beyond the seas.
Can there be any doubt then as to the opinion of these eminent gentlemen upon that point? But, because the right hon. the Prime Minister the other day quoted the opinion of Lord Milner with respect to the question of local defence, I will now quote from a later speech made by Lord Milner on the 20tli of April, 1909:
It is a real imperial navy, a navy constituted by the combination of the forces of the self-governing colonies, forces organized at the outset on a common pattern and controlled ultimately, as I hope, by a common authority. That is the goal towards which we should ultimately strive.
That being a later speech than the Prime Minister quoted, I think it would carry greater weight. Now let us see what the British admiralty themselves suggest as to the best means of meeting the emergency. Take first what is contained in the report of the imperial conference last July and I will read from page 23 to see whether this government have followed the suggestions of the admiralty:
In the opinion of the admiralty, a Dominion government desirous of creating a navy should aim at forming a distinct fleet unit; and the smallest unit is one which, while manageable in time of peace, is capable of being used in its component parts in time of war. Under certain conditions the establishment of local defence flotillas, consisting of torpedo craft and submarines, might be of assistance in time of war to the operations of the fleet, but such flotillas cannot co-operate on the high seas in the wider duties of protection of trade and preventing attacks from hostile cruisers and squadrons. . . . The fleet unit to be aimed at should, therefore, in the opinion of the admiralty, consist at lease of the following: 1 armoured cruiser (new ' Indomitable ' class, which is of the ' Dtead-nought ' type), 3 unarmoured cruisers (' Bristol ' class), 6 destroyers, 3 submarines.
Then at page 25:
As the armoured cruiser is the essential part of the fleet unit, it is important that an ' Indomitable ' of the ' Dreadnought ' type' should be the first vessel to be built in commencing the formation of a fleet unit.
In not one single one of these respects have the government followed the suggestions of the admiralty. They have not followed the suggestions of the admiralty as to a contribution which, if they were looking at the matter from a purely strategical standpoint, would be the best way of assisting to imperial defence. I do not blame

the government for not doing that, because I am not in favour of a fixed and stated compulsory contribution towards the maintenance of the British fleet. The next request is: If you will not do that, give us a fleet unit having at its head one of the most modern armoured cruisers of the Invincible and Dreadnought type. Have they done that? No, they have shorn the fleet unit of that which gives it its imperial aspect and that is the armoured Dreadnought. The little colony of New Zealand did follow the advice of the admiralty; she did give a Dreadnought. The Commonwealth of Australia did follow the advice of the admiralty, and she did give a fleet unit. Canada is the only colony that did not follow the advice of the admiralty. We gave neither a contribution, nor a fleet unit, nor a Dreadnought. In that respect we have neither followed the advice of the admiralty, nor that of the best men in the motherland who know what they are talking about and who say that we should at least contribute a fleet unit. Now, what have we got? We have got, or we are going to get, or it looks as if we were going to get, four Bristols, a Boadicea and some destroyers and submarines. The four Bristols that we are going to provide do not equal in tonnage, the one Dreadnought which we should have given. The four Bristols are not equal in lighting capacity to the one Dreadnought that New Zealand is giving, because the Bristols have only a tonnage of 4,800 tons as compared with one Dreadnought with a tonnage of 20,000 tons. There is no comparison between the guns of a Dreadnought and the guns of a Bristol. A Dreadnought will stand out there in the ocean while the four Bristols dare not go within firing distance. She is absolutely impregnable to the attack of a vessel of the Bristol class. Practically the only thing that the Bristol is good for is to act as a scout and see that the enemy is coming, and, if the enemy is coming, get out of her way as quickly as she can. Let us see exactly where we are. The minute that this fleet proposed by the right hon. gentleman comes into view the absence of an armoured head in the shape of a Dreadnought means: ' I do not pretend to be an imperialist.' 'Res ipse dixit.' The thing itself speaks. It says in effect: I do not pretend to be an imperialist, because the head and shoulders and fighting qualities of an imperial fleet have been lopped off by the right hon. gentleman. Notwithstanding this though the idea of the right hon. gentleman, according to his speech, was that in case of danger, from all points of the earth, the fleets of the colonies would rush upon the common enemy. We will suppose that the Armageddon has arrived. The call goes to Australia and up comes her fighting fleet unit with its armoured
head; the call goes to New Zealand and up comes its Dreadnought with its 20,000 tons armoured Dreadnought capable of putting our four Bristols out of commission. Then the call comes to Canada and up slinks her four unarmoured cruisers of the Bristol type to take their places in the battle line. We see Australia and New Zealand in the fore front, but where do we see Canada? We hear the officer in command of the naval squadron saying: Where are the armoured cruisers of Canada, where is the portion of the fleet which is going to do service on behalf of the empire?-and the answer of Canada is:	It is here. Where
are Canada's Dreadnoughts? Not here. Where is the balance of the fleet; where are the Bristols? The answer is: They are not here, either; they have slunk behind to get out of danger. Well, they cannot take any part in the battle. They are no match for Dreadnoughts, and because we cannot afford to waste the fighting power of our Dreadnoughts in their protection, they had better go back at 25 knots an hour from whence they came. If that Armageddon results in British victory they will be safe from further attack; but if the Armageddon results in disaster to our naval supremacy, then the victor will come to the shores of Canada and our fleet will have to show its heels at the rate of 25 knots an hour until it can show them no longer. But, as a matter of fighting force and efficiency in the defence of the empire these four Bristols are actually a negative quantity and, as our leader has said, in time of war, they are positively a danger and they would be better to be as far removed from the fighting line as possible. Then, the Postmaster General, for some reason-I do not know why-gave us a list of eighteen independent nations and self-governing colonies which have a population of less than 10,000,000 that have navies of their own. His illustration would have been good, I admit, if he could have pointed to self-governing colonies that have navies of their own. I do not know whether it was a mistake or not, but the statement made by the Postmaster General was this:
I have here a list of independent countries, and self-governing colonies, whose population does not exceed 10,000,000 people, and is in many cases less than that, who have navies of their own;
Then he gave a list of eighteen countries. On examining the eighteen countries he referred to as independent countries and self-governing colonies, I find that there is not a self-governing colony in the whole eighteen. If he cited that illustration for the purpose of proving that a self-governing colony ought to have a navy of its own, since there are no self-governing colonies in this list, the conclusion is that we do not need a navy; or, to put it in another way, we do need a navy because we in

Canada are going to be an indepedent nation. His illustration is absolutely without force unless he puts it on one of these two grounds, either that self-governing colonies have navies, and I have proved that there is no self-governing colony in this list, or that we are going to be an independent nation and need a navy.
Now, in conclusion, let me say that I have read very carefully the resolution which has been placed on the order paper by my honoured leader in amendment to the proposition of the government. I am thoroughly in accord with every proposition contained in that amendment. It repudiates the idea of non-imperialism and independence that pervades the whole policy of the hon. gentlemen opposite and also pervades the premier's speech in the introduction of the Bill. It makes provision for the impending necessities of the empire, which is the very reason that we are considering the Bill in question. It embodies the principle of effective co-operation on imperial lines, which is the only salvation of the empire, and, having satisfied the emergency, it gives the people the right to say what they shall do as to the permanent policy of this country with respect to naval questions. This is in line with the loyal, patriotic policy that has been advocated by the Conservative party within the memory of the oldest member of this House. So far as I know that policy is distinctively in line with the policy of the Conservative party on imperial matters. It is a policy which has for its hope and aspiration, not as the right hon. the Prime Minister says, that this country should sever its relations from the motherland as naturally as the ripe fruit falls from the parent tree, not that the goal of our ambition should be the independence of Canada, not that we as a child should leave the parent with a pang in her heart; not that, but it is in line with the idea that the undoubted position of this country should be that we should cultivate a sentiment of loyalty and devotion to the motherland, not only in ourselves but in those who shall succeed us, so that beyond all neradventure they will recognize that the destinies of this country are inseparably bound up with those of the empire. We have sufficient confidence and trust in the motherland to know that in her foreign policy she will always act in the same generous, magnanimous spirit which has actuated her in the past, and that she will never do anything that we need be ashamed of. We know that wherever the British flag floats order is restored, liberty is established, religious toleration prevails, education is fostered, and that peace, progress and development with their beneficial results inevitably follow in its wake. We know that the proudest boast of the Bo-Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
man citizen in the days when the world acknowledged the supremacy of Borne was: 'Civis Bomanus sum.' I am a Boman citizen, and if that was the proudest boast of a citizen of an empire far less great and noble than the British empire of to-day, how much prouder ought not we subjects of Britain be when we are able to say: 'Civis Brittanicus sum.' I am a British subject. But apart from all that there is this object lesson we ought to teach: That who ever meddles with the child meddles with the parent, and who ever meddles with the parent meddles with the child. That principle, Sir, is inconsistent with the declaration of the Prime Minister when he says: I do not pretend to be an imperialist. I say, Sir, that we cannot set a better example or precept than by passing the resolution proposed in amendment by my honoured leader, because its passage by this parliament will show the nations of the world that who ever meddles with the motherland must reckon with every part of the empire, and when that is thoroughly understood hostile nations will realize they are undertaking a herculean task. Let me conclude by quoting a few lines which I have taken the liberty to slightly paraphrase so as to adapt them to this phase of the question:
Ye who would reckon with Britain, Ye who would sweep from the seas, The flag that Rodney 'nailed aloft, And Nelson flung to the breeze,
Count well your ships, and your men, Count well your arms, and your guns, For they who reckon with Britain, Must reckon with Britain's sons.
