That is not surprising, however, in view of the fact that his restricted vision, owing to the political school in which he has learned his lesson and grown up in until this hour, prevents him from enjoying a proper appreciation of the life and purpose of the Liberal party in this great country. We are now in the last year of the first decade of the twentieth century, and during these ten years, and in fact for a bakers' dozen of years, the Liberal party has been in power in Canada under the leadership of the Bt, Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and, if the hon. gentleman

wants to know what is the policy of the Liberal party, I would refer him to the history of Canada during that period to which 1 have referred. Let him go to the statutes of this country, let him consider the marvellous development which has taken place in Canada in progressive legislation, in developing the natural resources of the country, in extending commerce, in attracting the attention of the British empire to our country; let him take into account the prominent place which Canada holds today, not only in the estimation of her own people, but in the estimation of the British public, and he will have something of a better definition before him of the life and labours of the Liberal party in Canada and the policy of that party as administered under the Prime Minister of to-day. Now, Sir, while Canada in one respect has a very short history, for our history proper began only in 1867 at confederation, we nevertheless have a history antedating that by some 300 years. And, let me say that if to-day we rejoice, as we have for some years past, in the possession of a free constitution-as free perhaps as that enjoyed by any people in the world-that constitution did not rain down from Heaven upon us. Sir, we have that constitution, and we enjoy it to-day because of the struggles of the Canadian people and largely because of the sacrifices of that portion of the Canadian people who have always been found within the bounds and limits of the Liberal party of Canada. Now, Sir, in this country we have had influences coming upon us from without as well as from within; we have not always had an easy course. We have gained our present position through stress and strain and struggle; we have had foes from without and sometimes enemies from within. 1776 is a date familiar to the members of this House as is 1812 and 1837-8 and .1866 and 1870, and the meaning of these dates have not been lost upon the people of Canada. Let me say, Sir, that because of the struggles, largely of those who stand as fathers of Liberalism in Canada we enjoy the free constitution under which the laws of this nation are being administered at this very hour, and one of the very distinctive principles of the Liberal party in the past has been that this nation should enjoy its freedom and autonomy within the empire and in the face of all the world. And, if to-day we stand as a growing and prosperous nation within the bounds of the British empire, no one presuming to dictate to us as to what our course shall be in any given particular, it is largely because of the fidelity of the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier to these principles of Liberalism which are embodied in the lives of those who are' known in history as the founders of the Liberal party. Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Middlebro) has undertaken to
defend the loyalty of the Canadian people, and he has spoken in particular of the loyalty of His Majesty's opposition in this House, and by inference he has endeavoured to create the impression that the Prime Minister of Canada is lacking in a proper spirit of loyalty towards the mother country at this present time. Sir, that hon. gentleman (Mr. Middlebro) will find that the task of Mrs. Partington with her broom endeavouring to sweep back the waves of the ocean, was a very pleasant pastime indeed in comparison with the efforts that he or others may engage in to endeavour to convince the Canadian people that the leader of the Liberal party is anything but a devoted subject of King Edward, as he is today the first son of Canada. And in no single particular is that fact more brilliantly displayed than in relation to this very naval programme which is under discussion at this moment.
Now, Sir, what are some of the things which help to determine a nation's destiny? One of these things surely is the possession of a national purpose. Have the Canadian people a national purpose? I feel that they have, and that national purpose is to achieve greatness in this greater half of the greatest continent of the world, with the government of which they are specially charged, and to maintain those ties and connections which have always in modern times bound us to the throne of England, and bind us at this hour. It was only yesterday that we passed from a state of tutelage, from a system of authority to a system of liberty. It is only very recently that we have felt our feet as a nation, and have begun to feel that we have a right to exercise all the privileges, duties, and responsibilities of nationhood; and to-day we stand on our own feel, ' the heirs of all the ages in the foremost flies of time,' and are willing to be judged on our merits. This is the spirit of the Bill submitted to the House by the premier. Mr. Speaker, under our representative system of government every man who sits in the House and who regards with any degree of seriousness his duty to those who have delegated him as their representative and his duty to the state at large must, or should, experience a constant sense of responsibility in the discharge of those duties, even during what may be called the routine work of parliament. But there comes times, and this essentially is such a time, when a peculiar and unusual responsibility rests on him. The party banner, the party cry, the party vote, necessarily, though perhaps too often dominate and determine the discussions in this Chamber. But there are some questions, and I think this is one of them, that should lose their 103J	*
party aspect when they come to be discussed.
This question, Mr. Speaker, was brought before this House on Thursday last by the leader of the government, and his speech in upholding the government policy was accorded a thoughful attention by members on this side of the House. I may perhaps be allowed for a moment to refer to a matter that I touched on in an earlier part of the afternoon. At the conclusion of the right hon. gentleman's speech outlining the policy of the government on the Naval Bill, the leader of the opposition also in a powerful and closely reasoned speech, at its close moved an alternative proposal which represents, as we believe, the best interests and wishes of the people of Canada. When he closed that speech, as we all very well remember, there was a spontaneous outburst of sentiment in this House, presenting a very unusual spectacle, namely, that hon. members stood up on their feet and sang the national anthem. That report in the recognized organ of the Liberal party in Canada, and in a great many affiliated papers, went out through the length and breadth of Canada; and it is perfectly natural for the people to think, assuming that that report was true, that my right hon. friend's speech was a speech not only of extraordinary merit, but that it must have created a great deal of enthusiasm on the opposition side of the House. Now, I am not taking the ground that because that report was incorrect the fault should be laid at the door of the press gallery in this House, because it may have been unintentional. Now, I think we all have a right to expect that the Prime Minister of Canada, in opening this debate, would have spoken in a manner worthy of the high subject with which he was dealing; but I say, and I say it emphatically, that it was amazing, it was disappointing, to find that, instead of starting out on that high plane showing a proper realization of the magnitude of the subject, he at once launched out in a manner so partisan, so small, that upon him must rest the responsibility of injecting Mr. BURRELL.
into this debate the party virus in its worst form. Now on that occasion, and on other occasions in dealing with naval matters, he has said a good deal about Rome. Let me bring to his notice a well worn word that describes the lofty patriotism which made Rome great in an hour of supreme danger, and will make any nation great:
Then none were for the party,
Then all were for the State,
Then the great man helped the poor,
And the poor man loved the great.
Then lands were fairly portioned,
Then spoils were fairly sold,
The Romans were like brothers In the brave days of old.
Well, was that the spirit in which the right hon. gentleman made the greater part of his speech? There was ridicule of our silence from the start, ridicule of the attitude taken by this side of the House, ridicule at our alleged indifference, spiced with jests to create laughter and applause, I was going to say upon his back benches, but it is rather significant that three of those back benches were empty during the whole of his speech. I say that nothing more narrow, more far removed from the spirit of true statesmanship, has been heard in this House than the speech of the right hon. gentleman. What do these tactics mean? Why does the Postmaster General follow suit? Why do they taunt us with being-I think the expressions used were Pharisees of imperialism, superloyalists, and the Postmaster General paraded his mock heroics about ' crimes committed in the name of loyalty.' We are familiar with these methods. Their unworthiness and their meaning cannot be hidden by floods of rhetoric in the peroration of minister's speeches. These tactics were adopted deliberately as a means of closing up their own ranks. Not once or twice, but many times we have seen the same thing. When lack of unanimity prevails amongst their followers when fatal weaknesses are exposed in a policy or in administration, my right hon. friend is astute enough to see that a wholesale charge that the Conservatives are attacking the great Liberal party is the best rallying cry to whip his own followers into line. Yet we must realize that a solemn and imperative duty faces every man, whether on the government or opposition benches, of deeply weighing the effect of his spoken works on this question, or even his silence, and of the vote which forms the final expression of his convictions.
The Bill now before parliament is a formal pronouncement of the government policy on a question of infinite importance -a question, which, in one shape or another, has been agitating the mind of the country for some time past. Above conflicting cries-and in spite of divergent

opinions, one great fact stands out strongly; Canada has evidently felt, and openly acknowledges, the vital-the	paramount
importance to Canada, of British naval supremacy, and the great need of a broad imperial unity.
Time was, and not so long ago, when he who raised his voice to urge Canadian duty in this high matter of assistance by the Dominion in the imperial naval defence was as one crying in the wilderness. It is now clear that in the hearts of a people, crowded with other pressing duties, this sense of responsibility this high sentiment did exist and in that moment when the note of danger, of trouble, was sounded across the seas a response was evoked from-the Atlantic to the Pacific which expressed in unmistakeable language the strength ol the popular convictions. This one thing then, amidst the many divergencies of opinion is at least clear gain. But Sir, the question, while in some respects con' cerned with the present day and hour, is not solely so concerned. To the rise, the development, the decadence of nations a vast number of factors, great and small, contribute, and as in the upper range of the mountains a pebble may deflect the course of a rivulet and determine its final destiny, so small, so obscure may be the causes which shape a nation's course and fate. But the student of history also knows that sometimes in national discussions the parting of the ways lies plain to the eyes, that some questions are so inevitably bound up with great issues that to fail to recognize their gravity is impossible.
Such a question is this now before the parliament of Canada. It is a time to speak out, a time to welcome the most absolute frankness of expression. There are some people-my right horn, friend the Prime Minister has expressed such an opinion-who believe that Britain's great colonies are destined to drop like the ripe fruit from the tree-a process of separation. I like better to take the simile of the family -the	clan-to believe that manhood
reached, the son while managing his personal affairs, is still of the family and the clan and inspired by a deep fealty springing from the ties of love and blood will unhesitatingly, in the face of a common danger, take his place by the side of his sire against even a world in arms.
The attitude of every man in this House towards the government proposals mu9t naturally be affected and his course in regard thereto be determined, first, by his views as to the imminence or non-imminence of danger to British naval supremacy and, second, bv his views on the general question of empire and Canada's part and lot therein, or whether indeed she is to deliberately shape her policy so as to
remain a permanent factor in that empire or assume a position of independence. One thing we have all agreed on, viz.-that the supremacy of the empire is essential, not only to its component parts but to the civilization for which that empire stands. The stability of England is the security of the modern world. Is that stability then threatened, and if seriously threatened, what is to be our attitude?
And, first, let me say, Mr. Speaker, that T do not share the anxieties of those who fear that the present time is marking the first steps of a decadent period in British history, that the old spirit which drove England to first place amongst the world powers is weakened; that her civilization, her polity is, in any sense of the word, moribund. It is true her problems are changing. We have witnessed a national struggle, indeed are still witnessing it, in which certain hysterical features seem to be noticeable, and prominence has been given for political purposes to phases in the national life far from beautiful, far from comforting. Nevertheless, those of us who have been long enough there to read beneath the surface of things realize the amazing vigour which characterizes the people of those small islands. It is treason to doubt, nor can we doubt, that the spirit which lies behind English liberties and English progress is as strong to-day as in past days. In the fiercest shock of adversity the cry will still be:
In the fell clutch of circumstance
I have not winced nor cried aloud,
Under the bludgeonings of chance
My head is bloody but unbowed.
Sixty years ago, in a time of trial, depression and fierce stress, England was visited by a clear-eyed, keen-brained son of the great republic to the south, probably her greatest son, as great at all events in intellectual as was Lincoln in state affairs. I refer, of course, to Ralph Waldo Emerson. His message, his words then have an absolute fitness to the present hour and are as true to-day as when he delivered them in Manchester in 1847.
And so, gentlemen, I feel in regard to this aged England, with the possessions, honours, and trophies, and also with the infirmities of a thousand years gathering round her, irretrievably committed as she now is to many old customs which cannot suddenly be changed; pressed upon by the transitions of trade, and new and all incalculable modes, fabrics, arts, machines, and competing populations-I see her not dispirited, not weak, but well remembering that she has seen dark days before; indeed, with a kind of instinct that she sees a little better in a cloudy day, and that in storm of battle and calamity she has a secret vigour and a pulse like a cannon. I see her in her old age, not decrepit, but young, and still daring to believe in her power of endurance and expansion. Seeing

this, I say. All Hail, mother of nations, mother of heroes, with strength still equal to the time; still first to entertain and swift to execute the policy which the mind and heart of mankind requires in the present hour.
But, Sir, though acquiescing in this great tribute to a great people we cannot shut our eyes to the far-sweeping changes which have come over the political and industrial map of the world since those words were spoken. The marvellous expansion of overseas Britain which has made the empire at once more strong and more vulnerable; the rise of an eastern nation to the rank of a first-class naval and military power, the tremendous development of the Pan-Germanic nations; these things necessitate a. new review of the world forces, and we in this great and growing Dominion have recognized at last that we cannot longer remain passive spectators, cannot longer abstain from offering our willing assistance in the work of consolidating the defences of the empire against any or all foes who might threaten that empire's integrity. First, then as to the question of whether there is imminent or real danger, for the answer to this practically determines our views as to what Canada should, or should not do at the present time. I take it that most of the members in this House have read the verbatim reports of the speeches delivered in the British House of Commons in March, 1909, the speeches especially of Mr. McKenna, the First Lord of the Admiralty. Mr. Balfour, and Sir Edward Grey. Any man who has done so and attached the weight to those grave and deliberate utterances, which they deserve, can hardly come to any other conclusion than that there was indeed an imminent danger to the empire, and I am aware of nothing having occurred since that time to make the situation less grave. Mr. McKenna's speech was delivered on the 16th of March, 1909, on the occasion of announcing the naval estimates, which were given as being in round numbers $175,000,000. His speech was the first official utterance following a certain unrest in the public mind as to a vastly increased naval programme on the part of Germany and following some expressioiis which suggested inadequate naval defence on the part of Great Britain. I quote one or two brief excerpts as bearing on this debate;
Our island position, the extent and dispersion of our empire; and the magnitude of our trade oblige us, as long as we are equal to the task, to maintain a navy adequate in strength to insure our shores from invasion, our empire from hostile attempts, and our trade from destruction in war.
In expressing his alarm at Germany's naval programme he added significantly:
We do not know, as we thought we did, the rate at which German construction is taking place.

Then, in relation to battleship construction, he further adds:
There vyill come a day when by an almost automatic process all ships of an earlier type than Dreadnoughts will he relegated to the scrap heap.
Mr. Balfour replied, couching his remarks in a manner, as admitted by the Prime Minister, entirely freed from party spirit and worthy of the .occasion. He stated:
We are face to face with a situation so new, so dangerous that it is very difficult for us to realize all that it imports.
Mr. Asquith followed, and hoped that the government would be able to lay down twenty Dreadnoughts to Germany's seventeen, by 1912.
In a leading article next day the ' Times ' referred to these speeches as containing ' utterances all serious and disquieting.'
These speeches were reported in the British press of March 17. On March 18, there appeared in the London ' Times ' a letter which not only by its power and ability, but from the fact that it came from the pen of an anti-militarist, a man well known in literary and philosophic circles, drove home the lesson of the day before with extraordinary force to the minds of the people of Great Britain. I refer, of course, to the letter of Mr. Frederick Harrison. Mr. Harrison starts by saying that his views were formed long before the recent discussions and were formed as the result of a long and careful study of European politics, and he explains with extraordinary power why he considered the problem facing the country as vital and urgent. In a brilliant and searching analysis Mr. Harrison pointed out that the Pan-Germanic ideal and its aim at hegemony was the obvious result of the European situation and of the history of Germany since the rise of Bismarck in 1864. He said:
The danger of collision lies not in any hostile disposition of the German people, but in the manifest tendency of the two dominant factors in world-politics-the military ascendancy and resources of the German empire face to face with the British empire based on command of the sea.
And he utters in conclusion this pregnant warning:
If ever our empire or our dominion of the seas is challenged, we now see that it will be no desultory attack in distant waters, not on India, South Africa, nor Australia

And he might have added Canada.

but by direct plunge at the heart of the
empire, on our arsenals, our ports and the capital.
Events followed in rapid succession. On the 22nd of March New Zealand, to her everlasting honour, cabled an offer to bear

the cost of building and arming a first-class battleship, and offered a second one if subsequent events showed it to be necessary. On the 25th of March'that offer was accepted. On March 29th, the very day in which a memorable debate took place in this House, Mr. Balfour moved a vote of censure on the government for not making adequate preparations, and though the government could not do otherwise than take the position that it was making due preparations, yet Sir Edward Grey, a statesman who commands in an exceptional degree the confidence and respect of the people, only confirmed general feeling as to the imminence of danger. We must all agree with his words that if the extravagant military and naval expenditures of Europe went on at the rate at which it had recently increased, it would sooner or later submerge the civilization on which it was a satire, and that the hopes and aspirations of the best men in the leading countries are devoted to trying to find some means of checking it. But we must also assent to his deliberate statement that to give up competition would be to sink into a position of inferiority, and if so, he added:
We should cease to count for anything in Europe; we should be fortunate if our liberty were left, and we did not become the conscript appendage of some stronger power.
In the closing words of his appeal to those on the ministerial benches not to oppose a generous naval programme, he admitted that:
We may be entering on a stage more grave, more serious, requiring greater care, greater effort than anything we have yet known.
Mr. Speaker, it is singular that at this very time, on the very night, as a matter of 'fact, that these grave warnings were uttered by one of England's most responsible statesmen, the Prime Minister of this government should have so little realized the gravity of affairs that he could speak as follows:
Let us not disguise the fact from ourselves that at present there is a passing wave in which we can trace anger, enthusiasm and fear, and which may be calculated_by some to force us to depart from our policy, and to contribute at once to the British navy. Let us view the question as it is, let us not blink at it, let us realize that it is not the way in which in the past we have understood our duty. This question is not new; we are familiar with it, it is not of to-day or of yesterday. I will not say it is old as the hills, but it is as old as confederation itself and it comes to the front periodically.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I had stated that there were two phases of this naval question-one, the question of the imminence or non-imminence of the danger to the naval supremacy, of the empire, and the other, the particular question of the empire and Canada's part or lot therein; and just according as each member regarded the weight to be attached to these particular questions, so would his whole attitude be on the proposals of the government. I had also quoted the utterances of responsible old country statesmen which were calculated to make the world at large, and especially us in Canada, believe that there was a serious menace to British naval supremacy; and I had further' stated that while nearly everybody was persuaded of this fact, while New Zealand had responded by presenting a battleship to Great Britain, the Prime Minister alone had remained practically unmoved. The right hon. gentleman did, it is true, acknowledge in a way that he has never done before, the obligations of this country _ to the empire and the necessity of upholding imperial supremacy, though even here his utterances were unnecessarily loaded with cautious warnings to preserve our autonomy. But it is apparent that he did not-grasp then, nor has grasped since, the vital fact of immediate danger and the accompanying necessity and duty of immediate assistance. Even the official organ of the Prime Minister's party, the Toronto 'Globe, has said on March 24, that German unfriendliness and aggression were apparent.
' War is deprecated,' said the ' Globe ' in its editorial:
But as a matter of fact war is in progress. The contest in shipbuilding is war. If the mother country were engaged in a deadly conflict Canadians could not get across the ocean fast enough to the aid of the motherland. But we must remember that our aid is as much needed now as if a physical war instead of a shipbuilding war were on. It is Canada's duty from every point of view, from our affection for the land of our fathers, and for our own self interest to take prompt and practical action.
Everybody sees imminent danger except the Prime Minister. He for his part said: ' I may say that we are not to be carried

away, we are not to be stampeded from what has been the settled policy and deliberate course which we have laid down, by any hasty, feverish action, however spectacular such action may be.' Well, Mr. Speaker, if the prompt giving of a battleship in the houT of English peril by the small colony of New Zealand be feverish and spectacular, thank God for a patriotism so spectacular, and let us all pray that we may be infected with a fever so sane ^ uplifting. And here a word may be said in regard to the resolution passed by this House on March 29, last, and which has been so much discussed since. It has been truly said by the leader of the opposition that unanimous action on the part of this parliament was so much to be desired, that it was eminently desirable that no vote should be taken which might seem to indicate a division on a subject of so much moment. It was a worthy sentiment, worthy of the lofty stand always taken by the hon. gentleman, who leads his Majesty's loyal opposition. But, Sir, it must also be said that though concurring with this view there were many members of this House who had a strong desire to go much further than that resolution, to put matters in such shape that immediate practical help should be at once forthcoming. I believed then, as I believe now, that the day will come when Canada might well undertake to do some efficient work in constructing or having constructed in her own ports, from her own wealth of natural resources, some substantial vessels to swell the fleet which patrols the empire, but I also believed then as I do more firmly now, that immediate effective help to the empire to which wre are so passionately attached could not come in that way. Much self-imposed restraint was necessary to avoid giving prompt expression to those views. But,- while we did refrain from generous motives, it has remained for the government and for the government press to make political capital out of that generosity by the attempt to pin us down to the narrowest meaning of that resolution and to meanly intimate to the country that we are at one with the government in its policy.
I have endeavoured to show that strong reasons existed for believing that British naval supremacy was threatened a year ago. The reasons are no less strong at this day and hour. The German naval budget estimates for 1910 are 443,000,000 marks, the largest in the history of the country, and they have within the past two weeks decided to borrow money to carry out with iron resolution and at all costs the enormous programme mapped out. It is singular, too, that within the last few months Britain has again been warned in impressive terms of her danger. In the heat of a political Mr. BURRELL.
contest the writings of Robert Blatchford have been lightly dismissed by those who had political reasons for so doing. But the message, graphic, stern, mercilessly logical m its marshalling of the facts, has gone home, and went home with additional force from the fact that again the sender of the message, Robert Blatchford, was not a jingo, not a panic monger, but a life-long antimilitarist. The Postmaster General has delivered some ex-cathedra utterances on the meaning of the late elections in Great Britain, and if he expressed himself half as freely in England as he has done in this House, one might have no difficulty in giving a local habitation and a name to the unknown, but semi-official authority quoted by the Manchester ' Guardian '' as expounding Canadian views on behalf of the Liberal party in Great Britain. Well, Sir, the minister, who seems to have taken such a keen interest in party politics in the old country, and whose ' peregrinations ' were paid for by the whole people of Canada regardless of party, will acknowledge that any word spoken by Lord Cromer is to be accorded some weight. This is not a party question. It is an imperial question. Let every commercial man in the empire understand that unreadiness for war means bankruptcy and panic and such suffering as this favoured people have never known. If I did not feel this strongly I would not say it. I am no longer young. I have had more than my share in unpopular causes. I would like to live a quiet life. The Postmaster General quotes the utterances of Mr. Asquith, Mr. McKenna and Sir Edward Grey on political plat-i forms. Not only do the whole of the Unionist votes testify to the truth of the facts as to danger to the empire, but it is unquestionably true that thousands also of those who support the Liberal or Labour party for other reasons would assent and do assent to the pressing need of strengthening British and imperial naval defence. I cannot see that there is offence to the German people in our position. My right hon. friend was a great admirer of Cobden, the man of peace. In the face of a threatened danger from another country, not half so serious as that which exists at present, Mr .Cobden said in 1861 :
I will vote a. hundred million pounds rather than allow the French navy to be increased to a level with ours, because I say that any attempt of that sort, without legitimate grounds, should argue some sinister designs on this country.

I hope I will be brief in the remarks which I intend to offer.

The Prime Minister and his colleague have expressed some pious sentiments in regard _ to their duty of defending British Columbia. urged that every member's attitude to this great question before the House must be determined by two things. But like thousands of my fellow-countrymen, I was born in England.- More than a quarter of a century ago, out of all the world, I deliberately chose Canada as my country. Does the Prime Minister subscribe to these opinions? No one doubts that we can assert our independence. Great Britain, as we read things, gives us full liberty, but earnestly asks full co-operation in welding the empire together. No longer dependence, but inter-dependence. The South African war was the final answer to those who shared or yet share Cobden's views. We want not a separated country, not a fleet which in the hour of danger may or may not lift a hand, or fire a gun, whose vessels according to a significant hint may be flying a distinctive flag, but we want one King, one fleet, one flag. I was amazed at a statement of the Postmaster General when he argued out these things. In his speech, arguing for the government programme, he said:
I have here a list of independent countries and self-governing colonies whose population does not exceed 10,000,000 people, who have navies of their own.
Sir, a review of that list is significant, for not a single self-governing colony is to be found in all the eighteen cases cited. Leaving out China, which the minister stated was contemplating a naval programme, we have the seventeen countries quoted. Of these Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Portugal, Holland, and Greece are monarchies. Let us glance at the rest and see how thi3 argument works out-an argument singularly unfortunate and even sinister: The Argentine Republic; Brazil, formerly a monarchy, but becoming a republic in 1889; Chili, which threw off the yoke of Spain and became independent in 1818; Colombia, which became a republic in 1819; Costa Rica, which took a similar course in 1829; Ecuador, a republic in 1830;Hayti, which asserted its independence in 1804, and, whose unhappy and stained history we all know; Mexico, which became independent in 1857; Paraguay, which threw off its allegiance to Spain in 1811; Peru, which also did so in 1821, and San Domingo, which became independent in 1844. Where are the self-governing colonies here? My hon. friend accused the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) of not playing the game fairly. What about this? Let it also be remembered that in becoming independent these countries, as far as naval services go, have found the result to be vast and ever-increasing expense, weak and inefficient navies and in many cases universal service.
Does the minister imply that we should cast off our allegiance as these countries have theirs? The term is of different import to us. Ours is not a yoke under which we give grudging service to tyranny, but an allegiance and a loyalty willingly given, willingly received and to sunder which would mean not independence, but final absorption by the great country to the south, whose history and development we admire, but whose problems are not ours, and whose political destinies we do not wish to share.
The Prime Minister has paid a tribute of admiration to Lord Milner and has sheltered his policy behind the words of that great imperialist. Long passages were read from Lord Milner's addresses in this country, addresses with which most of us are thoroughly familiar. My right hon. friend remarks:
Lord. Milner was here last fall, and you will pardon me, Sir, if I recall to the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite what were the opinions of Lord Milner upon this question.
He then cites amongst others the following passages from Lord Milner's Toronto speech:
It is not a question, of shifting burdens, but of developing fresh centres of strength. For this reason I have never been a great advocate of contributions from the self-governing states to the army and navy of the United

Kingdom, though as evidences of the solidarity of the empire such contributions are welcome and valuable pending the substitution of something better. But I am sure that the form which imperial co-operation in this field will ultimately take and ought to take, the form at once most consistent with the dignity of the individual states and most conducive to their collective strength and organic union, is the development of their several defensive resources in material and manhood.
Well, Sir, we too believe that regular and periodic contributions of money to Great Britain are not the most desirable way of performing our duty, and the leader of the opposition has said so very emphatically. We too believe that ultimately Canada should, and no doubt will, strengthen and develop her own defensive resources.. But let me emphasize one thing. Lord Milner was not in Canada last fall. This very address was delivered in October, 1908, and it is necessary, therefore, to clearly bear in mind, in arguing from the passages that the_Prime Minister quoted, that Lord Milner" was emphatically dealing with the ultimate policy, and not with what was Canada's best course at the present time.
What did Lord Milner, whose authority the Prime Minister invoked, say, when speaking on this question at Stockport on December 20 last? These words he uttered, and those who call him to their aid and shelter themselves behind his name and prestige would do well to bear them in mind:
The great position which this country occupied in the world-a position won for ns by the enterprise, sacrifice, industry and courage of our forefathers, though still held is being more menaced every day. The undoubted supremacy which this country at one time possessed at sea, if it has not gone, is seriously challenged.
We cannot doubt what the attitude of Lord Milner would be in the present case, nor can we doubt that he passionately hopes for a strengthening and not the weakening of imperial ties. My right hon. friend quoted a passage also from Lord Milner's speech in Vancouver in 1908. Here again it applies to ultimate action in defence and as the Prime Minister left off just where the passage became most interesting, I will finish the paragraph:
Without any loss of individuality, without any excessive strain on her resources it is within her power to enjoy all the benefits of that great position not only on this continent, but throughout the world, in which every selfgoverning community under the British Crown is equally entitled to participate. Canada would be greater, far greater, as a member, perhaps in time a leading member of that group of powerful though pacific nations, than she ever could be in isolation.
With that proposition we on this side of the House entirely agree, and it is because we agree to it that we cannot support a Mr. BURRELL.
policy which so obtrudes a false idea of autonomy as to say that a navy having been built, not a gun shall be fired until the Governor in Council or this parliament says so. The fundamental difference between military and naval matters in this connection are too obvious to be pointed out. Every one knows that on its naval side the issue between Japan and Russia was decided in the first hour of attack. The position taken by the government is impossible and repugnant to the feelings of the whole country. The moment, in the face of war, that question is debated that moment we cease to belong to the empire in any real sense. We cannot be of the empire and yet not of it. To say as prominent Liberal organs have said that we may lend our ships to Great Britain-with emphasis on the may-is to admit the point is an arguable one, a distasteful and dangerous admission.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding this expression of my own feelings on this great question. and also I believe the opinions of the vast body of my constituents, I can but again repeat my belief that the step proposed by the leader of the opposition is the wise, the patriotic, the right step and the people of Canada will so regard it.
We cannot lightly talk of war, or lightly consider the infinite miseries that follow it. Grant's words that 'war is hell' must remain true for ever. But there is another kind of war, a war which, to use the glowing words of Ruskin:
In which the natural instincts of self-defence are sanctified by the nobleness of the institutions, and purity of the households, which they are appointed to defend. To such war as this all men are born; in such war as this any man may happily die; and forth from such war as this have arisen throughout the extent of past ages, all the highest sanctities and virtues of humanity.
We owe it to ourselves to help the coming of that day when every state in the empire shall be worthily represented in a council of imperial defence. Such a step would in itself be the surest step towards the securing of peace. We owe it to ourselves in Canada at this time and hour to see that we linger not behind others in the defence of the empire.
On this grave matter, of a permanent naval policy, fraught with far-reaching results, the government ought and should consult the people who are the final authority. We know not whither it will lead, or what consequences will follow: 'Once to every man and nation comes the moment to decide'. If the Prime Minister will not refer the issue to those who placed this government in power, we can at least tell him what we feel to be the absolute truth: that Canada,
