if it were given its rightful opportunity of expression, its choice between the government proposals and the patriotic plan of the leader of the opposition-would unhesitatingly choose the latter, and, out of its riches, and out of its strength, sustain a policy which makes for the speedy and effective strengthening of that navy which has guarded our liberties in the past, and which alone can guard them effectually in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell), for a gentleman who bestows so much contempt upon waves of enthusiasm, certainly to my mind gave undue importance at the beginning of his remarks to the exact chronological moment at which he and his followers in somewhat discordant tones, so far as I can remember, sang the National Anthem. I have been accustomed to hear Tories on both sides of the Atlantic claim a monopoly of loyalty and patriotism, and it would now seem as if they claimed a monopoly of the National Anthem. I am one of those, Sir, who do not believe that the main strength and enduring greatness of a people depend upon armaments. The world is full of decayed civilizations, but every one of these civilizations died first from within. The real strength of a people is in the strong arm, the healthy body, but far more than that in a healthier mind and good morals. And, I am bound to say that the people of Canada, following as they have followed, the advice of the right hon. the Prime Minister -which has been suitable for Canada up to this period of her history-the advice to keep out of the vortex of European militarism, have not lost but gained in the process. Does any one pretend that Canada has been weaker because she has followed1 that policy hitherto? No. With no desire to interfere with others and yet with a quiet determination that others shall not interfere with her, the strength of Canada has been as the strength of ten because her heart was pure. But, having said this much I am bound to admit that we live in a practical age and that the resolution of last March really narrows this discussion down to a very fine point indeed. It narrows it down to two definite lines of policy upon which we must decide. As the House, most unfortunately as I think, upon a question of foreign policy is to be forced to a division. Now, I think it would be regarded as a presumption on my part were I to make a long speech. I do not think that the House or the country is looking for long speeches from private members after the extremely exhaustive speech of my right hon. frienid the Prime Minister on the second reading of the Bill and the equally exhaustive speech of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition on the first
reading. I would like, however, to say a few words on the points which have been raised in the speeches of the two gentlemen who have spoken for the opposition to-day; and at the outset I wish to say that I am in perfect agreement with the main position taken by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) and by the hon. member for Yale Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) as to what ought to determine, or largely determine, the attitude of members on this question. The question, is there any immediate peril to the empire? Is that peril imminent or non-imminent? as my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo put it, is a question upon the answer we give to which will depend largely the attitude of members who want to give a rational vote at the end of this discussion.
Now, both my hon. friends have based their case for a present imminent peril of the empire very largely upon what I'may call authority. One of the authorities was quoted with very great surprise to me. I am surprised that my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo attached the importance he did to the writings of the quondam Socialist, Mr. Robert Blatchford. Why, Sir, if he were well acquainted with the former writings of that gentleman-perhaps he is, I do not know, but it does not seem to me as if he were-he would remember that Mr. Blatchford, when he was the editor of a paper called ' The Clarion,' eight or ten years ago, was writing in that paper the very stuff about a German invasion which he has been trying to frighten the British public with during the general election. If that be the kind of authority on whom my hon. friend bases his effort to prove that the German menace is imminent, and if that gentleman has been blowing his clarion off and on for the last eight or ten years, and we are still living free from a German attack, I am bound to say that my logical faculties are such that I cannot be worked into a state of panic over anything that emanates1 from the pen of Mr. Robert Blatchford. However, there were very-much more eminent authorities quoted by my hon. friend from North Grey as well as by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo. A great deal was made by the hon. member for North Grey of the speeches delivered to our own delegates and the delegates from the rest of the empire on the occasion of the press conference in Great Britain last summer. But as I listened to the quotations from those speeches, so far as I could gather the object of the various statesmen speaking to those press delegates, they did not want to convey to them for a moment that there was any particular peril to Great Britain at the hands of Germany. I think they rather wanted to impress upon them a thought as old as Adam Smith, that the time had come when the whole burden of imperial defence could no longer be allowed

to rest on the mother country. Take the language that was used. The members of the press conference were asked to exercise a- forethought extending over years, to look forward, and Mr. Balfour was careful to say to the delegates that there should be no panic.
A great deal was made by both of my hon. friends of the utterances of Sir Edward Grey. I quite agree with them that no British statesman could be quoted whose language ought to be listened to with greater respect or consideration than that of Sir Edward Grey. But I think that where my friends have made a mistake is that they have not seen the most recent utterances of that right hon. gentleman. Speaking when the election was almost over, at Hexham, in my native county, after seven seats fought there had gone Liberal, and contributing his quota to the eighth one going Liberal, he referred to his speech of last March, which my hon. friends have quoted, and referred to it in this language:
There was not a word to take from anything from which they said in March last with regard to the navy, and not a word to be unsaid. Was there anything to be added? Yes, this, that during last year they gave orders for the ships which were necessary to be built to be put in hand in the course of this year in order to maintain our naval position. In March they said that it might require to be done; they were now in a position to say that they had done it.
Well, that is one member of the British Cabinet; and let me say at this point that I cannot confine myself in what I quote to utterances preceding the late general election. I was astonished at my hon. friend the leader of the opposition taking that attitude, because it surely created the inference that no men of front rank in British politics are quite sincere at election times. Well, I do not concede that. I think I can furnish evidence that some candidates in the recent campaign were sincere; and, while we may believe in the sincerity of Mr. Robert Blatchford, I do not think we need attach much importance to what he said. But when Mr. Lloyd-George, who was the leading figure in the recent contest, and who will continue to be a leading figure in political life in England for years to come, described this, like other British panics, as ' manufactured cries of national danger,' I think we should attach some importance to his language. Mr. Asquith, shortly after the speech on which my hon. friends base so much of their reasoning, went on to add that old ladies of both sexes might rest quietly in their beds, because the empire was perfectly secure. Now, I contend that such a description, applied to the scare mongers is sufficiently strong, and comes from a sufficiently high authority, for a country with our broad' prairies and our

clear air and our self-reliant people not to pay too much attention to these scaremongers. Mr. Churchill, another prominent member of the British Cabinet-and these are men who know the real condition of the navy-has referred to the scare-mongers of last spring as ' March hares and April fools running about the country creating an unfounded panic.' But before this House had broken up in the month of May last, another prominent member of the British Cabinet was doing what many of the British people were doing at intervals during the most of last summer-interchanging ideas with their fellows of the same race among the great German people. The right Hon. John Burns was addressing a large number of German trades unionists who were visiting Great Britain, and he used this language:
Your visit is timely. It coincides with the collapse of an attempt to foment mischief between the two great branches of the same race. I have seen a few scares in this country come and go, but I never saw one more hollow and less decent than the last. It has hardly lasted the traditional nine days. It was confined to a small section of people, and I may say, with few exceptions, to the least reputable of our journals, to the most unreliable of our precocious politicians, and to a few socialists who ought to have known better.
That was very strong language to have ci me right on the back of the scare on which we carried the resolution of last March and on which scare, I understand, the whole defence of the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is being based by the two speakers who have preceded me to-day. But we are not (dependant on British authority in this matter. I hold in my hand the account of the Press Conference, by one of the ablest journalists in Canada, who was present at that conference, written in England in the shape of letters to his own newspaper while there. And what had he to say about the scare in the country last summer while the conference was going on? If the speeches quoted by the hon. member for North Grev (Mr. Middlebro) had the significance which he attached to them, surely that significance would have found its way into the head of this journalist.
Who was that journalist?
Mr. John Dafoe, the editor of the Manitoba 'Free Press.'
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends laugh at the name. I suppose that is because he belongs to a different political party than themselves. I described him as a great journalist, and if I want to justify

my description of him I could surely do it up to the hilt when I mention that there was scarcely a committee of the journalists for whatever purpose of that conference appointed by themselves on which Mr. John ,Dafoe was not placed, and let me say to my hon. friends that when we have the good opinion of our peers and fellows with whom we work we have the highest testimony that we are men of reputation and of worth. Mr. Dafoe said:
The panic, of course, has quite passed away, leaving behind it a fixed resolution in the minds of Englishmen, of all classes, that in a matter of such supreme importance to them as the supremacy of the seas, they will take no chances.
Might I offer the testimony of another journalist who has passed through the recent election. I think that, as Canadians, we cannot afford not to pay attention to the journalists who are over there. Something was said by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) in criticism of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) for a remark he made about the last elections having settled the war scare, and the hon. member for Grey in regard, to that, quoted Portsmouth as a place where the scare was evidently believed in. In Portsmouth and the other dockyard towns: it is not so much belief in the scare as our old and well known friend, patronage, which affects an election. It is a cure for the scare that the people of Portsmouth and Davenport are interested in, because they get their living by building ships, and, of course, they listen to any one who goes there and promises an enlarged naval force. Mr. Joe Clark is the correspondent to whom I refer. I do not remember even the papers which he represented, but I read all his letters, and his forecasts of the campaign seem to me to indicate a journalist of an alert mind to whose word we should attach a good deal of importance. He said:
The navy scare will probably pass away. In fact it lias been almost impossible to find anybody not on the stump afraid of Germany and one feels that such talk would, not be used except in a country too strong to care whether a neighbouring nation took offence or not.
Mention was made of Lord Beresford's attitude. This same journalist quotes some words of Lord Beresford, and I am bound to believe he would only have done so on the best of authority. He states that Lord Beresford said after the contest, and I think these words indicate the exact importance he attached to the scare:
I do not wish to make a party thing of the navy, but you have got to get into parliament somehow.
Taking these views of the journalists who have been there and the leading mem-104
bers of the British cabinet, I am bound to say that I do not see there is much evidence that they believe in any imminent danger from Germany at all. I would like to quote the language of Mr. Balfour, the prominent statesman on the other side of politics. He was taken to task by Mr. Asquith for referring to an opinion among the statesmen and diplomatists of the lesser powers of Europe. Mr. Balfour said:
You will find among them absolute unanimity of opinion that a struggle sooner or later between this country and Germany is inevitable.
Yes, but Mr. Balfour was careful, with the sense of responsibility which naturally is felt by a man who might conceivably have had to go into office and hold diplomatic- relationships with the great country of Germany, to immediately add:
I do not agree with them, that is their opinion.
So that every leading member of the government of England, at the present moment. has thrown doubt upon the motives and the reality of the scare of last spring, and Mr. Balfour, the leader of the opposition, agrees with them.
But, as I said, my friends have rested mainly upon authority in this matter. I, Sir, have other methods bv which I judge of the importance of these panics into which the British people go from time to time. A little history is a splendid cure for a good deal of hysteria. I am old enough, I regret to say, to remember when the word ' jingo ' first became a current word in British politics. In 1878 Lord Beaconsfield and the Marquis of Salisbury returned from the Berlin congress, and the Prime Minister made the famous speech in which he said: I bring you peace, and peace with honour. The London crowd went crazy and broke Air. Gladstone's windows. Yes, but the London crowd was not then representative of British opinion, and in 15 or 16 months after that event, so far from the British people being carried away by that panic and entering or rather coming any nearer to war with Russia-it was Russia that the scaremongers were frightened of at that time-Mr. Gladstone won the country by a majority of 120, and that scare, for the moment, was forgotten, indeed it has been forgotten ever since because we have 'had no war. It is over half a century ago since the British people were similarly excited over the absurd rumour that the French people were building ships secretly in the harbours of Toulon and Cherbourg. There is no one to whom we ought to pay the attention that we do to the successful prophet, the man who sees the meaning of those things at the time. As I said, a little history is a splendid cure for a good deal of hysteria. Mr. Richard Cobden said at that time:

There is something very puerile in the recent attempts to frighten the country with stories about secret preparations in the French dockyards.
Yes, and how puerile it looks to us today, 50 years after the event, when we reflect that from that moment to this there has grown up between the great French and English nations the entente cordiale unbroken by a single warlike act during half a century.
It is absurd to have any fears of a war between Germany and England at the present time, owing to the relative strength of the two peoples and the two fleets. Why, I do not understand the make-up of the Jingo. It is beyond all possible doubt that the British seamen in the British navy at the present time number two and a fraction to one in the Germany navy. Britain is equally superior in the matter of ships. What is the attitude of lion, members towards the Englishman's fighting power anyway? The people who made the charge at Balaclava did not ask to be twice as strong as their opponents? I 'have never heard that Nelson and Wellington made it a sine qua non of their fighting that thev should be two and a half times as strong as the enemy. I cannot understand the make-up of the Jingo. Have hon. members no belief in the might of England? Have they no knowledge of her history? I cannot for the life of me see why we should insist on Britain being two and a half times as strong as Germany, and, when we fear that it may be otherwise, to get into a state of hysterical excitement and do things that we shall be sorry for six months after when we have recovered from our unworthy panic. But I rest more on the good-will that prevails between the two peoples. And I am bound to say that, while I think a number of my fellow countrymen have been-to use the old American phrase-twisting the tail of the German lion, a trick that used to be played regularly in elections in the United States with regard to Great Britain herself, it redounds greatly to the credit of the German people that they have taken it all calmly and quietly. Thq trade relations between the two peoples make it the most unthinkable thing in the world that there could be war between them. Let me read what John Burns1 said on this subject upon the occasion to which I have referred:
On the ground of race, religion, ideals and aims, Europe and the world would he the poorer if Germany and Britain were involved in a war. Germany was England's best customer and he was not a wise shopkeeper who advocated the blacking of the eyes of his best customer as a means of advertising his business. England sent Germany over £41,000.000 of goods and Germany sent England £57,000,000 a year, £12,000,000 of which was in food, whilst Mr. M. CLARK.
the British empire sent to Germany goods to the value of £90,000,000.
It is inconceivable to me that the two foremost nations of the world to-day are going to stop the whole beneficial service of commerce in the North Sea to fight it out like two school boys to see which is the stronger of the two.
Now, Sir, I think I have furnished sufficient ground for holding a different view from that of these two hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred as to the imminence of the German peril. But, we are face to face with the situation, peril or no peril, and there are two methods of handling it before the members of this House. Now, I must say that I was immensely disappointed when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) tabled his amendment. Having regard to the speeches which he had been delivering all summer and during the fall, I anticipated that he would allow this question of the foreign policy, this question of such immense importance, to pass the House without a division. We have heard, however, Sir, that the tail sometimes wags the dog. When three tails of extraordinary activity get wagging all at one time the result is likely to be serious. The result was the production of what I would call an omnibus resolution-an omnibus with compartments. Into one compartment was hustled the -hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) and those who agree with him, singing: 'We don't know where we are, but we're going to the countrv to find out'. Into the more roomy compartment of the omnibus were crowded the larger number of those who sit behind the leader of the opposition, singing, as befitted them, the old Jingo refrain:-
We don't want to fight,
But, by jingo, if we do,
We've got the men, and we've got the ships,
And we've got the money, too!
Until my hon. friend resumed his seat, I thought there would have been a compartment for the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), but he struck on the business and switched off on a little conveyance of his own. The main omnibus was driven, I need not sav. by the leader of the opposition with everv apparent encouragement from his chief lieutenant, and the_ whole party raced off as fast as they could from implementing the resolution for which they were, equally with the other side, responsible last March.
What is it that the amendment proposes, Mr. Speaker? It proposes to carry out at once the policy of the opposition and propose to refer the oolicv of responsible government to the people. Well, that is a shifting of governmental respon-

sibility. But, if a referendum is good for the Liberal policy, which happens to be the policy of the majority of this House, surely it will be equally good for the policy of the minority, especially as there is no great panic, as I have tried to prove. Surely, the referendum policy wo.uld apply to the policy of providing Dreadnoughts as well as to the proposal to build a Canadian navy? There are one or two questions which I would like to ask about the giving of these Dreadnoughts. How often would hon. members propose this policy? Are these Dreadnoughts to be the finish, the final policy of Canada? Is that all they propose to do towards saving the empire in the midst of the terrible peril to which she is exposed in the pages of Mr. Robert Blatchford's writings? If not, and if there is to be gift of Dreadnoughts, when? I wish to push these questions upon the opposition. 1 judge that there will be plenty of members from that side following me, and I want them to explain to the House and country just how this thing is going to work out. How many Dreadnoughts are we going to give? Perhaps I could help to answer that question. These delegates of ours to the imperial conference saw a wonderful sight in the Solent last summer. The British fleet was there assembled, 144 battleships, covering eighteen miles of water. And the thing which bears upon the question I am putting to my.hon. friends of the opposition is this

that only one of these battleships had been in existence twelve years before. You are going to give two towards one hundred and forty-four-not an almighty contribution, but probably sufficient There are a great many questions that the opposition have been directing to the government side of the House about, the government policy that are equally applicable to their own. What is the empire going to do. we have been asked, during the time the ships are building? All I have to .say is that if the empire, with 144 ships of hey own on the Solent, depends absolutely for her salvation upon the two Dreadnoughts of the opposition, she will be in a worse place still. But the point I wish to urge upon my hon. friends is that this fleet was new within twelve years. You give your two Dreadnoughts, at a cost to Canada of about $25,000,000. Then, about time when the British fleet is rebuilt, you have to give two Dreadnoughts again. But if, long before that, Mr. Robert Blatch-ford and the yellow press of England agree to raise a scare, are you going to propose a policy of this kind every time such a scare is raised? There is a great deal to be said in support of my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) -when he said that the yellow press was at the back of this whole policy. I hold in my hand a telegram sent February 29, 1909, from the 1041
' Standard ' newspaper in England to the 'Evening Journal' of this city:
Build your navy. The rest must come. Build and your claim to a share in controlling imperial defence cannot be evaded, but build.
Now, I would like to know if, every time the English yellow press gets into this particular mood, and sends a telegram to the ' Evening Journal ' of Ottawa, we are going to give another couple of ' Dreadnoughts ' ? Unless we are to withdraw from the empire altogether, you are not going to stop with the two, you will give another couple at least in eight or ten years when the present vessels of the British navy have become obsolete, and you have to replace them. But during that time you will not have taught a single Canadian to go to sea without- being sea-sick, you will not have taught a single Canadian youth to walk the decks, yon will have remained a nation of land lubbers-that is the practical outcome of the policy of the opposition. Contrast that with the plan of the government. The panic on one side, what we are concerned with is, not the giving of ' Dreadnoughts,' not a policy which is so ill thought out as that, but we are concerned with the orderly development of Canada as a portion of the empire.
Now what are the merits of the government plan? 1 want to state them in a couple of sentences. In the first place, the government plan is at least on an equality, for emergency purposes, with the opposition plan, because, if we are going to have a war with Germany next week, it is clear that any money we send to build [DOT] Dreadnoughts ' could not be used in that time. So that so far as emergency goes, the one plan is as good, or as poor, as the other. If emergency comes upon Britain quickly, we should at any rate be in quite as good a position as the opposition, or as we have been at any past period in British history. But I would say in criticism of the hon. leader of the opposition at this point that the very objection he made to the government plan is equally applicable to his own: it either goes too far, or not far enough. For my part, if the empire were really in danger, I do not believe Canadians would be content with giving a couple of ' Dreadnoughts.' The real "asset which the empire has in Canada is in the knowledge of the fact that behind her, if the worst comes to the worst, she has all the material and moral resources of the people of Canada; and when that is made known to her it is better than giving a couple of ' Dreadnoughts.' So far as emergency goes, that is all the knowledge that Britain would want. I have some young fellows myself who can handle a rifle fairly well, and if the old land was really exposed to danger from a foreign foe, those young fellows, and others in the west, could not be restrained, and I think

I	should have to put a sticking plaster on myself. ' Give a couple of Dreadnoughts.' I have heard of little Englanders in England, and I think I have discovered some little Canadians in Canada.
Not only is the government plan at least on an equality for emergency purposes with the opposition view, but it guarantees the autonomy of Canada. Now, disguise the contribution plan as yoir may, it gives away that autonomy, and if you repeat your contribution from time to time, it becomes equivalent to taxation. If you do not repeat it, then I think you would be little Canadians. Disguise it how you may, a cash contribution for ' Dreadnoughts ' would amount to taxation without representation. Now, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, running away as he was from his resolution of last March-because it was his just as much as the Prime Minister's-he did what is very uncommon with him, but he did what people very often do when they are going to do a foolish thing, he rather lost his temper, and he charged the right hon. gentleman with great heat, with having talked two-thirds of the time he was on his feet, wide of the subject. Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with that view. I think that the magnificent argument we had, the history we had of the rise of Canadian autonomy, and the need of preserving it, was absolutely pertinent to that point. What is the history of the colonies of the empire in that respect? From the time of Lord Durham's memorandum and the repeal of the navigation laws by Lord John Russell, the attitude of the old country has been under the aegis of British Liberalism; the policy of the old country has been to produce, not so much an empire, as an alliance of free naltions, independent for a great many purposes, but connected for others. That is the history of autonomy, and I should think that our Tory friends would have had enough of the other policy when they reflect upon what happened to the United States of America. That good old Tory. Lord North, believed in running the colonies from Downing street, and he tried it with the American colonies, with the re-mlt that they are gone. Well might Lord Beaconsfield call the Tory party the stupid party, because they are talking the same imperialsm to-day, they are building the same kind of a Tower of Babel, that will end in the same confusion, and chaos, and failure that attended that memorable building.
Not only is the government plan on an equality' for emergency purposes with the opposition plan, not: only does it guarantee the autonomy of Canada, but as I have said, it takes its place naturally in the national development, and it. keeps hold of the purse strings. Let me say, Sir, that this is a point of very great, importance. My Mr. M. CLARK.
hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo said just now that the Lord loveth a cheerful giver. Well, it is as well that he quoted that text for the benefit of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, because I am sure it would never have any effect upon the Minister of Finance. ' The Lord loveth a cheerful giver ' may be a very good maxim for people to carry out in their private enterprises, but I do not think it would be a good maxim for those responsible for taxing the country, and governing the people with the proceeds of their taxation. The Lord may love a cheerful giver, but I do not think the taxpayer has the same affection for him. I am bound to say that the resolution of last March could not leave this country where it had been, because we were bound after that resolution to do something. A great deal of the growth of this nation's responsibility in the empire is based upon the possibility of paying our own obligations as we go along, and retaining some of the benefit by giving fresh outlets to the enter-; prise of our people; and if we are ever to be a sea-faring people, teaching our young generation, those of them who want to go to sea, to learn to be sailors, would seem to be an essential part of a sound policy upon this question. I have endeavoured, as far as might be, to argue this question, free from partisanship.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

Well, if a man be a partisan when he proves that the authorities of those who build up a panic are not quite what they expected they were themselves, then I have been a partisan. I have taken one side of the argument, but it happens to be the right side. I have, at least, been non-partisan in this that I have never hinted, nor would it be fitting to hint, at the want of loyalty on the part of a single member of the Conservative party. Be he French or English, I give him credit for as good citizenship as I possess myself, and I must say that it would redound greatly to the credit of the Conservative party if they would follow my example in that respect. I marvel at any member of the Conservative party trying to cast doubt, upon the First Minister of the Crown of this great country. I marvel at it for this reason that for two generations Liberalism has been teaching that the peculiar glory of the British people has been that they are colonists and -that they can take Frenchmen and, by giving them their freedom, make them good citizens of this great free empire. It is still the glory of British statesmen and of British Liberalism to believe in freedom as the cement of empire, witness the giving of freedom recently to South Africa. I marvel at this want of courtesy and want

of faith. However, I recollect that before I became a citizen of Canada I used to see that when the Prime Minister visited Britain, at least, his loyalty was believed in there by all classes, of the people. I tell my hon. friends with all due deference to the talent which is on their benches, that it will be a long time before the same kind of a reception is given to any man outside of the right hon. gentleman himself in Great Britain.
Sir, if, after over 200 years of freedom from war in Great Britain, the smoke of battle were to be seen there again instead of the much more beneficent smoke of industrial enterprise which has prevailed for a couple of centuries, and if the land of this sacred island were to be stained again with human blood, from all I have seen of Canadians, I believe there would be aroused the cry from the whole Anglo-Saxon population of Canada: Hands off the cradle of our race, but I believe there would be mingled with that cry the equally patriotic and strong cry from every one of our French Canadian citizens:	Hands off the
mother of our liberties.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I may say that I do not propose to treat this subject at any great length, but there are a few points to which I desire to direct attention. I listened somewhat attentively to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who has just taken his seat for the purpose of jotting down points that I might answer, but I regret to say that the paper is yet a comparative blank. Although he travelled over ancient, medieval and modem history, political economy and the .abstract questions of government, nearly four-fifths of his speech, I thought, had very little to do with the question before the House. He did say before he sat down that the Canadian people were loyal. Well, I agree with him in that. I think there is no doubt about that. The Canadian people as a whole are loyal. There may be individual cases of disloyalty. There may be policies propounded for Canada that, if carried out, would lead to disloyalty, but I think the great heart of the Canadian people is loyal. The hon. member for Red Deer finished by saying that the government proposal or plan had two merits. What were they? One was that it was quite as good as that proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). Well, that is an admission that there is some merit in the proposal contained in the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. He did not claim that the government proposal was any better, but at least that it was as good. The other merit w^as that it preserved the autonomy of Canada. Does that imply that the amendment which was proposed would not preserve the autonomy
of Canada? That is the only and natural inference to be drawn from the hon. gentleman's remarks. There is no man in this House who will read the resolution calmly and dispassionately, or analyse and criticise it fairly, who will reach the conclusion that there is anything in it that would lead to a sacrifice of the autonomy that we enjoy at the present time. The hon. gentleman went over a lot of ground and what occurred to me as a fair summing up of his speech as a whole was what i heard once from a very young professor who was asked if he could give a clear and logical demonstration of chemistry. Well, he said, the shortest and best that I know of is about this. I will give you an example of it:
You take air effervescent And add a deliquescent.
There will be a precipitation
That is a conglomeration
That amounts to a demonstration.
His statement was just about as clear and just about as logical. The first observation made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when moving the second reading of the Bill, which attracted my attention, was the positive and emphatic statement, as he turned around to look at his friends^ that the government intend to stand or fall by this policy. What did he intend that to be? It could not be addressed to members of the opposition because they are generally found opposing the government, but it was a very strong and vigorous threat addressed to his own friends. Why? Because forsooth there must be a very great diversity of opinion and strong opposition to the policy which the government has propounded. That is the only conclusion to reach from that observation. I am justified in reaching that conclusion as well, because farther on, in answer to the question I asked him: Do you mean to say that when England is at war, Canada is at war?-he said: Certainly he did. Then he went on to say that when he made that statement he shocked his friends in Quebec until they rent their garments and tore their hair. These remarks were addressed to his friends in Quebec, and it, therefore, would not seem that they were standing as a solid phalanx behind his back; they could not have been addressed to the opposition in this House because he does not stand or fall by the power of the opposition, for were they strong enough they w-ould vote him out of power. Then his next observation was that there v'as no emergency between Germany 'and England. Surely to arrive at this conclusion he must have ignored the calm and deliberate statements made by Sir Edward Grey, by Mr. Reginald McKenna, by Air. Asquith, by Lord Roberts, by Lord Char-
32c?3

les Beresford, and every one of the public men of England who gave their views- as to the necessity for a strong naval construction policy by Great Britain. True, the Postmaster General told us, when I questioned him across the floor, that he was ignorant of the statements made by these gentlemen last spring, but he had heard the matter discussed during the election. However that may be, surely the Prime Minister was aware of the statements of British statesmen that there was a grave crisis at present in the British empire. The right hon. gentleman told us that if there was any emergency the Liberals would be as ready to assist in the time of need as the Conservatives would be, but if all he has heard and seen will not convince him that a crisis is- upon the empire, then it would be a waste of time for us to try to convince him. The right hon. gentleman told us there was no danger because the navy of England represented 2.000,000 tons displacement, whereas the German navy represented only 890,000 tons. That may be all very well when you apply it to each of the navies as -a whole, but if you take from the British navy such ships as are not considered of any great- value as a fighting force, and then compare the Dreadnoughts of the two countries, the difference will not be found to be nearly so great. If Germany should continue her activity in building Dreadnoughts for the next three or four years, and if England should make no more progress than she has made for some years past, then Germany would have a fighting force equal to that of England. And, if this great German navy is not intended against England, what does she want it- for? No other naval power than England begins to compare with her. England is the only country that- has a navy superior to that of Germany, and if Germany did not design her ships against England she would have no nation with which to claim rivalry on the seas. The right hon. gentleman t-old us that it was trifling with common sense to say that this policy now announced by the government was "a new policy, and he added that it had been clearly before the people since 1902. Well, there were three distinct colonial conferences attended by representatives -of Canada. At the first conference all that was done was to agree to have another conference in three years. The second conference was largely taken up with discussion as to the trade relations between the different portions of the empire, and although defence was mentioned there was nothing formulated except the assistance offered by the Australian colonies to the motherland. At the conference of 1902 there was a proposal made in regard to naval defence, and one of the authorities who made the statement before the conference said:

to these there is an army of clerks, attached to the department involving an expense of several thousand dollars each year in addition.
I have given these figures to show what the new undertaking will involve in a few years. Instead of being able to handle that militia force with $16,000, we now require $73,000. I believe to-day it is over $100,000 and is increasing every year. When I first spoke on this, I said it was the commencement of militarism, and I repeat the same thing with regard to the present proposal of a naval force. It is the commencement of militarism that the Canadian people dread because of the expense involved in it and the little result that will accrue to the country. For that reason, I say, I am opposed to it because, I believe, it is radically wrong. I am opposed to it because it does not meet the present emergency. What did the people in England say was required to meet the present emergency? They said:
If the problem of military and naval defence were considered merely as a problem of naval strategy

And naval strategy is what gives them control of the high seas to-day, with a force standing at their back.
it would be found that the greatest output of strength for a given expenditure is obtained by the maintenance of a single navy with the concomitant unity of training and unity of command.
That is what would be the most valuable.
In furtherance then of the simple strategical ideal the maximum of power would be gained if 'all parts of the empire contributed, according to their needs and resources, to the maintenance of the British navy.
That is what would do the most good. If our desire is to do the most good to strengthen the British navy, surely we ought to have some regard to their expert knowledge, to their judgment and to their views, and they tell us that is what they desire; but .we are told Canada will never consent to that. It is said that if we gave in that way it would be taxation without representation. Perhaps it would be and yet after all it might not be a bad thing, and we might be able to do that without any injustice to Canada and with great good to the British empire. But that is the judgment of the British people and I say I am opposed to this because it does not meet the present emergency. In no sense or in no way can it meet the present emergency. Now it is said that the emergency is on, we must either deal with it or do nothing, and that if it matures at the present rate it must come to a head within a few years. The Prime Minister himself said that these ships could not be built, we could not have a ship ready to go into com-

mission before at least five years. But a navy to be of any value would take at least 15 years to build. What is to become of the emergency in the meantime? What assistance are we giving to the British fleet in the meantime? None whatever, and that emergency is on. that emergency must be met.
England said: If the colonies will not assist we are bound to do it ourselves. She accepted courteously and thankfully the offers made by New Zealand, Victoria and the Australian Commonwealth generally when they offered ' Dreadnoughts ' and money-but Canada made no offer, Canada stood aloof from it. Therefore, I say, I am opposed to the proposal because it does not meet the present emergency. I have no doubt many in this House have noticed that for several years past a proposal has been made by the foremost minds of the world, that the different nations should have a conference and agree to" a limitation of their naval and military forces, and their expenditures for the development of these forces. Almost every nation in the civilized world has offered to agree to it except Germany. While Germany has said she was willing to agree to it, she was never prepared to do it. In the meantime, while she was professing a desire to control her naval expenditure, she was still going on spending more and more each succeeding year.
She must have had some purpose. What was that purpose? England was ,ready to go into that conference, France proposed to go into it; even the United States was prepared to go into it-all civilized countries were prepared to enter the conference except Germany. But Germany was going on building her Dreadnoughts and preparing for her naval battle whenever it came. If, to-day, the colonies of the empire came to the assistance of England with a gift of money which she could use in aceoi'dance with the well-matured plans that her naval experts have evolved from generation to generation, her force would be increased to the greatest extent and in the quickest way, and England would be ready to cope with Germany. Germany then might regard it as useless to go on. developing her naval forces as she has been doing. And, if she reached that conclusion, she might go into that conference and decide to limit hex-naval and military expenditure. If this were done, the enxergency would be over. Giving once, we might not be called upon to give again. This would be a free gift, on the saxxxe lines as our sending men to take part iix the South African war. It would not be taxation without representation; it would be a free and voluntary gift, and, as the enxergency might not arise again for many veax-s, we might save ourselves the millions upon nxillioxxs which we must

spend to go on with a navy as proposed at the present time.	_
I am opposed to this policy, because it was not what the British naval authorities suggested would be of the most use to them. They said that a naval unit -would be the best contribution outside of money. The fighting they said must be done bv Dreadnoughts, while the smaller craft are good in their way they are practically of no value in the work for which the Dreadnought is needed. There fore, we are not preparing to give what the naval experts of England said every colony should give that wished to help the empire in the best way. It is suggested that with Esquimalt and Halifax to care for, if we want to have a naval force of any value and to look after these ports, we must have a force on the Pacific and one on the Atlantic. But. because the government is not prepared to undertake that expenditure, it cannot provide a single unit, the only fighting force that Britain thought would be of great value. But a monev con tribution would meet the emergency. Therefore, I would favour a monev contribution, which, as I have. said, might be required onlv once in a generation.
And lastly, I am onposed to this policy because the Canadian people have not had an opportunity to express their views upon it. The government has never submitted their policy to the people either by referendum or at a general election. I hold that we should not commence such an undertaking without asking the judgment of the Canadian people upon it, and if the government is not prepared to evolve a policy and submit it to the Canadian people at the next general election, they are not the kind of statesmen as are to be found in every other portion of the British empire except Canada. For this would be in accordance with the principle of our form of constitutional government-the government propounds its policy crystallizes it into form and submits it to the people and asks for their approval.
Might I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) if he would propose to put off submitting the question until the next general election?

What I would propose to do is exactly what I have said. The government should give a contribution either in money or in vessels in order to meet the present emergency. We might not require to do that again for a long time. Then, they should evolve a policy and submit it to the Canadian people, either by calling a general election, or by making it an issue in the next general election, and let the people express their views upon it. When that is done, when the Canadian people endorse the policy, the administration will be justified'in going on with it; if they do not endorse it, it will have to be abandoned for the future. For these reasons, I am opposed to this Bill and in favour of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition.
